# Erlang OTP Standard Library — Complete Module Reference

**Version: OTP 29 / stdlib 8.0**

---

## 1. `lists` — List Processing

**Category:** Collections / Sequences
**App:** stdlib

The foundational list-processing module. All functions are purely functional; lists are singly-linked.

**Functions:**

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `all/2` | Returns `true` if predicate holds for every element |
| `any/2` | Returns `true` if predicate holds for at least one element |
| `append/1` | Concatenates a list of lists |
| `append/2` | Concatenates two lists (equivalent to `++`) |
| `concat/1` | Concatenates text representations of atoms/integers/floats/strings |
| `delete/2` | Removes first matching element |
| `droplast/1` | Removes last element |
| `dropwhile/2` | Drops elements while predicate is true, returns rest |
| `duplicate/2` | Returns list of N copies of a term |
| `enumerate/1,2,3` | Pairs each element with its index |
| `filter/2` | Keeps elements satisfying predicate |
| `filtermap/2` | Filter + transform in one pass |
| `flatlength/1` | Length of flattened deep list |
| `flatmap/2` | Map then flatten one level |
| `flatten/1,2` | Fully flatten a deep list |
| `foldl/3` | Left fold (tail-recursive) |
| `foldr/3` | Right fold |
| `foreach/2` | Iterate for side effects |
| `join/2` | Inserts separator between elements |
| `keydelete/3` | Delete by key in Nth position of tuple list |
| `keyfind/3` | Find tuple by key in Nth position |
| `keymap/3` | Map over Nth element of tuple list |
| `keymember/3` | Test membership by key |
| `keymerge/3` | Merge two key-sorted tuple lists |
| `keyreplace/4` | Replace tuple by key |
| `keysearch/3` | Find tuple by key (legacy; prefer `keyfind`) |
| `keysort/2` | Sort tuple list by Nth element (stable) |
| `keystore/4` | Replace or append tuple by key |
| `keytake/3` | Extract tuple by key, returns rest |
| `last/1` | Last element |
| `map/2` | Transform every element |
| `mapfoldl/3` | Map + left fold in one pass |
| `mapfoldr/3` | Map + right fold in one pass |
| `max/1` | Maximum element by `>=` |
| `member/2` | Test element membership |
| `merge/1,2,3` | Merge pre-sorted lists |
| `merge3/3` | Merge three pre-sorted lists |
| `min/1` | Minimum element |
| `nth/2` | Nth element (1-indexed) |
| `nthtail/2` | Tail starting at position N+1 |
| `partition/2` | Split into {Satisfying, NotSatisfying} |
| `prefix/2` | Test if List1 is prefix of List2 |
| `reverse/1,2` | Reverse (optionally with tail) |
| `search/2` | Find first matching element |
| `seq/2,3` | Generate integer sequence |
| `sort/1,2` | Sort (optionally with custom comparator) |
| `split/2` | Split at position N |
| `splitwith/2` | Split at first element failing predicate |
| `sublist/2,3` | Extract sub-sequence |
| `subtract/2` | List difference (remove first occurrences) |
| `suffix/2` | Test if List1 is suffix of List2 |
| `sum/1` | Sum of numeric list |
| `takewhile/2` | Take elements while predicate holds |
| `ukeymerge/3` | Unique merge by key |
| `ukeysort/2` | Sort + deduplicate by key |
| `umerge/1,2,3` | Merge + deduplicate |
| `uniq/1,2` | Remove duplicates (stable order) |
| `unzip/1` | Split list of pairs into two lists |
| `unzip3/1` | Split list of 3-tuples into three lists |
| `usort/1,2` | Sort + deduplicate |
| `zip/2,3` | Zip two lists into pairs |
| `zip3/3,4` | Zip three lists into 3-tuples |
| `zipwith/3,4` | Zip with combining function |
| `zipwith3/4,5` | Zip three lists with combining function |

```erlang
%% Basic operations
lists:map(fun(X) -> X * 2 end, [1,2,3]).      % [2,4,6]
lists:foldl(fun(X, Acc) -> X + Acc end, 0, [1,2,3,4,5]). % 15
lists:filter(fun(X) -> X rem 2 =:= 0 end, [1,2,3,4,5]).  % [2,4]
lists:partition(fun(X) -> X > 3 end, [1,2,3,4,5]).        % {[4,5],[1,2,3]}
lists:keysort(2, [{a,3},{b,1},{c,2}]).         % [{b,1},{c,2},{a,3}]
lists:seq(1, 10, 2).                           % [1,3,5,7,9]
lists:enumerate([a,b,c]).                      % [{1,a},{2,b},{3,c}]
lists:uniq([1,2,1,3,2]).                       % [1,2,3]
lists:zipwith(fun(A,B) -> A+B end, [1,2,3], [4,5,6]). % [5,7,9]
```

## 2. `maps` — Hash Map / Dictionary

**Category:** Collections / Key-Value
**App:** stdlib (since OTP 17)

The primary key-value store. Implemented as hash array mapped tries (HAMT). Keys compared by match (`=:=`).

**Functions:**

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `new/0` | Empty map |
| `put/3` | Insert or replace key |
| `get/2` | Get value (raises `{badkey,K}` if missing) |
| `get/3` | Get value with default |
| `find/2` | Get as `{ok, V} \| error` |
| `update/3` | Update existing key (raises if missing) |
| `update_with/3` | Update with fun (raises if missing) |
| `update_with/4` | Update with fun or insert default |
| `remove/2` | Remove key (no-op if absent) |
| `take/2` | Remove + return value |
| `is_key/2` | Membership test |
| `keys/1` | List of all keys |
| `values/1` | List of all values |
| `size/1` | Number of associations (O(1)) |
| `merge/2` | Merge two maps (Map2 wins on conflict) |
| `merge_with/3` | Merge with combiner fun |
| `intersect/2` | Keep only common keys (Map2 value wins) |
| `intersect_with/3` | Intersection with combiner |
| `filter/2` | Keep pairs matching predicate |
| `filtermap/2` | Filter + transform |
| `map/2` | Transform all values |
| `fold/3` | Fold over all pairs |
| `foreach/2` | Iterate for side effects |
| `from_list/1` | Build from `[{K,V}]` |
| `from_keys/2` | Build from key list, all same value |
| `to_list/1` | Convert to `[{K,V}]` |
| `with/2` | Subset by key list |
| `without/2` | Remove keys by list |
| `iterator/1,2` | Create iterator (optionally ordered/reversed/custom) |
| `next/1` | Advance iterator |
| `groups_from_list/2,3` | Partition list into map of groups |

```erlang
M = #{name => alice, age => 30},
maps:get(name, M),                        % alice
maps:get(missing, M, default),            % default
maps:update_with(age, fun(V) -> V+1 end, M), % #{name=>alice, age=>31}
maps:filter(fun(K,_) -> is_atom(K) end, M),  % #{name=>alice,age=>30}

%% Grouping
maps:groups_from_list(
  fun(X) -> X rem 2 end,
  [1,2,3,4,5]).
% #{0=>[2,4], 1=>[1,3,5]}

%% Ordered iteration
I = maps:iterator(#{b=>2, a=>1}, ordered),
maps:to_list(I). % [{a,1},{b,2}]
```

## 3. `sets` — Hash Set

**Category:** Collections / Set
**App:** stdlib

Unordered set with no duplicates. Default implementation since OTP 28 is a hash-based structure (version 2). Elements compared by match (`=:=`). Compatible interface with `ordsets` and `gb_sets`.

**Functions:**

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `new/0,1` | Empty set (optionally specify version 1 or 2) |
| `add_element/2` | Insert element |
| `del_element/2` | Remove element |
| `is_element/2` | Membership test |
| `is_empty/1` | Empty test |
| `is_set/1` | Type check |
| `size/1` | Cardinality |
| `union/1,2` | Set union |
| `intersection/1,2` | Set intersection |
| `subtract/2` | Set difference |
| `is_disjoint/2` | True if no common elements |
| `is_subset/2` | Subset test |
| `is_equal/2` | Equality test (works across versions) |
| `from_list/1,2` | Build from list |
| `to_list/1` | Convert to list (unordered) |
| `filter/2` | Keep elements matching predicate |
| `filtermap/2` | Filter + transform |
| `map/2` | Transform all elements |
| `fold/3` | Fold over elements |

```erlang
S1 = sets:from_list([1,2,3,4]),
S2 = sets:from_list([3,4,5,6]),
sets:to_list(sets:union(S1, S2)),        % [1,2,3,4,5,6] (any order)
sets:to_list(sets:intersection(S1, S2)), % [3,4]
sets:to_list(sets:subtract(S1, S2)),     % [1,2]
sets:is_subset(sets:from_list([3,4]), S1). % true
```

## 4. `ordsets` — Ordered Set (sorted list)

**Category:** Collections / Set
**App:** stdlib

Sets represented as sorted lists. Elements compared by `==` (not `=:=`). O(N) operations but ordered and list-interoperable.

**Functions:** (same interface as `sets`)

`new/0`, `add_element/2`, `del_element/2`, `is_element/2`, `is_empty/1`, `is_set/1`, `size/1`, `union/1,2`, `intersection/1,2`, `subtract/2`, `is_disjoint/2`, `is_subset/2`, `is_equal/2`, `from_list/1`, `to_list/1`, `filter/2`, `filtermap/2`, `map/2`, `fold/3`

```erlang
S = ordsets:from_list([3,1,4,1,5,9,2,6]),
ordsets:to_list(S). % [1,2,3,4,5,6,9]  -- sorted, deduplicated

%% Note: ordsets uses == not =:=
ordsets:is_element(1.0, ordsets:from_list([1])). % true (1.0 == 1)
sets:is_element(1.0, sets:from_list([1])).        % false (1.0 =/= 1)
```

## 5. `gb_sets` — General Balanced Tree Set

**Category:** Collections / Set
**App:** stdlib

Sets backed by AVL-like balanced binary trees. O(log N) operations. Elements compared by `==`. Good for ordered traversal and range queries.

**Functions:**

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `new/0` | Empty set |
| `empty/0` | Alias for `new/0` |
| `add/2`, `add_element/2` | Insert |
| `delete/2`, `del_element/2` | Remove (raises if absent) |
| `delete_any/2` | Remove (no-op if absent) |
| `is_element/2`, `is_member/2` | Membership |
| `is_empty/1` | Empty test |
| `size/1` | Cardinality |
| `union/1,2` | Union |
| `intersection/1,2` | Intersection |
| `subtract/2`, `difference/2` | Difference |
| `is_disjoint/2` | Disjoint test |
| `is_subset/2` | Subset test |
| `from_list/1`, `from_ordset/1` | Build from list/ordset |
| `to_list/1`, `to_ordset/1` | Convert to sorted list |
| `filter/2` | Keep matching elements |
| `fold/3` | Fold in ascending order |
| `next/1` | Iterator step |
| `iterator/1` | Iterator (ascending) |
| `iterator_from/2` | Iterator starting at element |
| `largest/1` | Maximum element |
| `smallest/1` | Minimum element |
| `take_largest/1` | Remove and return max |
| `take_smallest/1` | Remove and return min |
| `balance/1` | Rebalance tree |

```erlang
S = gb_sets:from_list([5,3,8,1,9,2]),
gb_sets:smallest(S),      % 1
gb_sets:largest(S),       % 9
gb_sets:to_list(S),       % [1,2,3,5,8,9]  -- sorted

%% Ordered iteration
I0 = gb_sets:iterator(S),
{V1, I1} = gb_sets:next(I0), % {1, ...}
{V2, I2} = gb_sets:next(I1), % {2, ...}

%% Range: all elements >= 4
I = gb_sets:iterator_from(4, S),
gb_sets:next(I). % {5, ...}
```

**Category:** Collections / Key-Value (ordered)

Key-value store backed by AVL-like balanced trees. O(log N) all ops. Keys compared by `<` (Erlang term order). Ordered traversal available.

| Function | Description |

| `keys/1` | Sorted list of keys |
| `values/1` | List of values in key order |
| `to_list/1` | List of `{K,V}` in key order |
| `from_orddict/1` | Build from orddict |
| `size/1` | Number of entries |
| `is_empty/1` | Empty test |
| `map/2` | Transform values |
| `iterator/1` | Iterator (ascending) |
| `iterator_from/2` | Iterator starting at key |

```erlang
T0 = gb_trees:empty(),
T1 = gb_trees:insert(b, 2, T0),
T2 = gb_trees:insert(a, 1, T1),
T3 = gb_trees:enter(c, 3, T2),

```

## 7. `queue` — Double-Ended FIFO Queue

**Category:** Collections / Queue
**App:** stdlib

Efficient amortized O(1) enqueue and dequeue from both ends. Implemented as a pair of lists.

**Functions (three APIs coexist):**

**Original API:**
| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `new/0` | Empty queue |
| `in/2` | Enqueue at rear |
| `in_r/2` | Enqueue at front |
| `out/1` | Dequeue from front → `{{value,V}, Q} \| {empty, Q}` |
| `out_r/1` | Dequeue from rear |
| `peek/1` | Inspect front without removing |
| `peek_r/1` | Inspect rear |
| `is_empty/1` | Empty test |
| `len/1` | Length (O(N)) |
| `member/2` | Membership test |
| `to_list/1` | Convert to list |
| `from_list/1` | Build from list |
| `reverse/1` | Reverse queue |
| `join/2` | Concatenate two queues |
| `split/2` | Split at position N |
| `filter/2` | Keep elements matching predicate |
| `filtermap/2` | Filter + transform |
| `fold/3` | Fold front to back |

**Okasaki API:** `cons/2`, `head/1`, `tail/1`, `snoc/2`, `last/1`, `daeh/1`/`liat/1`

```erlang
Q0 = queue:new(),
Q1 = queue:in(a, Q0),
Q2 = queue:in(b, Q1),
Q3 = queue:in(c, Q2),
{{value, a}, Q4} = queue:out(Q3),
queue:to_list(Q4).  % [b, c]

%% Dequeue from both ends
Q = queue:from_list([1,2,3,4,5]),
queue:peek(Q),   % {value, 1}
queue:peek_r(Q). % {value, 5}
```

| `strip/1,2,3` | Trim both ends (legacy) |
| `prefix/2` | Strip matching prefix → rest \| nomatch |
| `slice/2,3` | Extract substring by grapheme position |

```erlang
%% Unicode-correct length
string:length("hello").      % 5
string:length(<<"héllo"/utf8>>). % 5 (é is one grapheme)

%% Split/trim
string:split("a,b,,c", ",", all). % ["a","b","","c"]
string:trim("  hello  "),         % "hello"
string:trim("xxhelloxx", both, "x"). % "hello"

%% Case
string:to_upper("héllo"). % "HÉLLO"
string:casefold("Straße"). % "strasse"

%% Find
string:find("hello world", "world").    % "world"
string:prefix("hello world", "hello"). % " world"

%% Jaro similarity
string:jaro_similarity("kitten", "sitting"). % ~0.746
```

```erlang

binary:split(B, <<" ">>),              % [<<"hello">>, <<"world">>]

binary:match(B, <<"world">>),          % {6, 5}
binary:part(B, 6, 5),                  % <<"world">>
binary:replace(B, <<"world">>, <<"there">>). % <<"hello there">>

%% Numeric encoding
binary:encode_unsigned(1024),          % <<4, 0>>
binary:decode_unsigned(<<4, 0>>).      % 1024
```

## 15. `unicode` — Unicode Encoding/Conversion

**Category:** String / Binary
**App:** stdlib

Encode/decode between Unicode representations: UTF-8, UTF-16, UTF-32, and Erlang's internal codepoint list format.

**Functions:**

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `characters_to_binary/1,2,3` | Convert to UTF-8 binary (or specified encoding) |
| `characters_to_list/1,2` | Convert to codepoint list |
| `bom_to_encoding/1` | Detect BOM and return encoding |
| `encoding_to_bom/1` | Get BOM bytes for encoding |

Returns `{incomplete, Converted, Rest}` or `{error, Converted, Rest}` on failure.

```erlang
unicode:characters_to_binary("héllo"),    % <<"héllo"/utf8>>
unicode:characters_to_list(<<"héllo"/utf8>>), % [104,233,108,108,111]

%% Explicit encoding
unicode:characters_to_binary("hello", utf8, utf16).
% <<0,104,0,101,0,108,0,108,0,111>>  (UTF-16 big-endian)

%% BOM detection
unicode:bom_to_encoding(<<16#EF, 16#BB, 16#BF, "rest"/utf8>>).
% {utf8, 3}  -- BOM is 3 bytes
```

| `scan_format/2` | Scan format control sequences |
| `unscan_format/1` | Inverse of `scan_format` |
| `build_text/1` | Build iolist from scanned format |
| `deep_char_list/1` | Test if deep character list |
| `printable_list/1` | Test if printable character list |
| `printable_unicode_list/1` | Test if printable Unicode list |
| `nl/0` | Newline iolist |
| `tab/1` | Tab iolist |
| `char_list/1` | Type check |
| `flatten/1,2` | Flatten iolist to string |

**Format directives:** `~w` (write), `~p` (print), `~s` (string), `~d` (integer), `~f` (float), `~e` (scientific), `~g` (shortest float), `~i` (ignore), `~n` (newline), `~N` (platform newline), `~t` (unicode), `~lp` (limit depth)

```erlang
io_lib:format("Hello ~s, you are ~p years old~n", ["Alice", 30]).
% [72,101,108,108,111,32,65,108,105,99,101,44,32,...]

%% Useful pattern: flatten to string
lists:flatten(io_lib:format("~w", [{a,b,c}])). % "{a,b,c}"

%% fread (scanf-style)
io_lib:fread("~d-~d-~d", "2024-01-15").
% {ok, [2024, 1, 15], ""}
```

## 17. `io` — I/O Server Interface

**Category:** I/O
**App:** stdlib

All terminal and file I/O in Erlang goes through I/O server processes. `io` is the API to these servers.

**Functions:**

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `format/1,2,3` | Formatted output (to device or stdout) |
| `fwrite/1,2,3` | Alias for `format` |
| `write/1,2` | Write term |
| `print/1,2` | Pretty-print term |
| `nl/0,1` | Write newline |
| `put_chars/1,2` | Write raw characters/binary |
| `get_chars/2,3` | Read N characters |
| `get_line/1,2` | Read line |
| `read/1,2,3` | Read and parse Erlang term |
| `scan_erl_exprs/1,2,3,4` | Tokenize Erlang expressions |
| `scan_erl_form/1,2,3,4` | Tokenize a complete Erlang form |
| `parse_erl_exprs/1,2,3,4` | Parse Erlang expressions |
| `parse_erl_form/1,2,3,4` | Parse a complete Erlang form |
| `setopts/1,2` | Set I/O device options (e.g., `binary`, `unicode`) |
| `getopts/1` | Get I/O device options |
| `rows/0,1` | Terminal row count |
| `columns/0,1` | Terminal column count |
| `request/2` | Low-level I/O request |
| `requests/2` | Multiple I/O requests |

```erlang
io:format("~p~n", [{hello, world}]).     % prints {hello,world}\n
io:format(standard_error, "Error: ~s~n", ["oops"]).

%% Reading
{ok, Term, _} = io:read("Enter term: ").

%% I/O to a string (via string device)
{ok, Dev} = file:open([], [write, read]),  % not ideal; use io_lib instead
```

**Open modes:** `read`, `write`, `append`, `exclusive`, `raw`, `binary`, `{encoding, unicode}`, `compressed`, `{read_ahead, Size}`, `{delayed_write, Size, Delay}`

```erlang
%% Read entire file
{ok, Bin} = file:read_file("/etc/hostname"),

%% Write file
file:write_file("/tmp/test.txt", <<"hello\n">>),

%% Open and stream
{ok, Fd} = file:open("/tmp/test.txt", [read, binary]),
{ok, Data} = file:read(Fd, 1024),
file:close(Fd),

%% Consult Erlang terms
%% File contains: {key, value}. [1,2,3].
{ok, Terms} = file:consult("data.erl"),
% Terms = [{key, value}, [1,2,3]]

%% File info
{ok, Info} = file:read_file_info("/tmp"),
Info#file_info.type,  % directory
Info#file_info.size.
```

## 19. `filename` — Path Manipulation

**Category:** I/O / File System

| Function | Description |

| `absname/1,2` | Absolute path |
| `absname_join/2` | Absolute path + join |
| `basename/1,2` | Last path component (optionally strip extension) |
| `dirname/1` | All but last component |
| `extension/1` | File extension including `.` |
| `rootname/1,2` | Strip extension |
| `join/1,2` | Join path components |
| `split/1` | Split into components |
| `pathtype/1` | `absolute \| relative \| volumerelative` |
| `flatten/1` | Flatten deep path iolist |
| `nativename/1` | Platform-native separator |
| `safe_relative_path/2` | Guard against directory traversal |
| `find_src/1,2` | Find Erlang source file |
| `find_file/2,3` | Find file in path list |

```erlang
filename:join(["/usr", "local", "bin", "erl"]). % "/usr/local/bin/erl"
filename:basename("/usr/local/bin/erl"),          % "erl"
filename:basename("/foo/bar.txt", ".txt"),        % "bar"
filename:dirname("/usr/local/bin/erl"),           % "/usr/local/bin"
filename:extension("file.beam"),                  % ".beam"
filename:rootname("file.beam"),                   % "file"
filename:split("/a/b/c"),                         % ["/","a","b","c"]
```

| Function | Description |

```erlang
filelib:wildcard("*.erl"),            % ["foo.erl", "bar.erl", ...]
```

## 22. `rand` — Pseudo-Random Number Generation

**Category:** Math / Numbers
**App:** stdlib

Multiple PRNG algorithms. State can be process-local (implicit) or explicit. **Thread-safe when using explicit state.**

**Algorithms:** `exsss` (default, Xorshift116**), `exsp`, `exs1024s`, `exro928ss`, `splitmix64`, `mwc59`

**Functions:**

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `seed/1,2` | Seed the process PRNG |
| `seed_s/1,2` | Seed and return explicit state |
| `export_seed/0` | Export current state for serialization |
| `export_seed_s/1` | Export explicit state |
| `uniform/0` | Float in `[0.0, 1.0)` |
| `uniform/1` | Integer in `[1, N]` |
| `uniform_s/1,2` | Explicit-state versions |
| `uniform_real/0` | Float with full mantissa precision |
| `uniform_real_s/1` | Explicit-state version |
| `integer/1` | Integer in `[0, N-1]` (since OTP 26) |
| `bytes/1` | Random binary of N bytes |
| `bytes_s/2` | Explicit-state version |
| `normal/0,2` | Normal distribution |
| `normal_s/1,3` | Explicit-state normal |
| `jump/0,1` | Jump ahead in sequence |

```erlang
rand:uniform(),          % e.g. 0.7421
rand:uniform(100),       % e.g. 42  (integer 1..100)
rand:bytes(16),          % 16-byte random binary

%% Reproducible: explicit state
S0 = rand:seed_s(exsss, {1,2,3}),
{V1, S1} = rand:uniform_s(100, S0),
{V2, _S2} = rand:uniform_s(100, S1),

%% Normal distribution
rand:normal(0.0, 1.0).  % mean=0, stddev=1
```

```erlang
Port = erlang:open_port({spawn, "cat"}, [binary]),

```

## 24. `timer` — Timer Utilities

**Category:** Process / Concurrency
**App:** stdlib

Convenience wrappers around `erlang:send_after/3` and `erlang:start_timer/3`. Uses a gen_server internally.

**Functions:**

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `sleep/1` | Block current process for N milliseconds |
| `tc/1,2,3` | Measure execution time → `{MicrosecondTime, Result}` |
| `send_after/2,3` | Send message after N ms |
| `send_interval/2,3` | Send message every N ms |
| `apply_after/3,4` | Call MFA after N ms |
| `apply_interval/3,4` | Call MFA every N ms |
| `cancel/1` | Cancel timer |
| `start/0` | Start timer server (called automatically) |
| `hours/1` | N hours in milliseconds |
| `minutes/1` | N minutes in milliseconds |
| `seconds/1` | N seconds in milliseconds |

```erlang
timer:sleep(1000),  % sleep 1 second

{Time, Result} = timer:tc(lists, sort, [[3,1,2]]),
% Time = microseconds, Result = [1,2,3]

Ref = timer:send_after(5000, self(), timeout),
timer:cancel(Ref),

%% Periodic
timer:apply_interval(timer:seconds(30), io, format, ["tick~n", []]).
```

## 25. `calendar` — Date and Time

**Category:** Time
**App:** stdlib

Date and time arithmetic. Erlang's native datetime format is `{{Year,Month,Day},{Hour,Minute,Second}}`.

**Functions:**

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `local_time/0` | Local datetime |
| `universal_time/0` | UTC datetime |
| `now_to_local_time/1` | `erlang:now()` timestamp to local datetime |
| `now_to_universal_time/1` | Timestamp to UTC datetime |
| `local_time_to_universal_time/1,2` | Local to UTC |
| `universal_time_to_local_time/1` | UTC to local |
| `datetime_to_gregorian_seconds/1` | Datetime to seconds since year 0 |
| `gregorian_seconds_to_datetime/1` | Inverse |
| `date_to_gregorian_days/1,3` | Date to days since year 0 |
| `gregorian_days_to_date/1` | Inverse |
| `time_to_seconds/1` | Time tuple to seconds since midnight |
| `seconds_to_time/1` | Inverse |
| `day_of_the_week/1,3` | Day number (1=Monday..7=Sunday) |
| `is_leap_year/1` | Leap year test |
| `last_day_of_the_month/2` | Days in month |
| `valid_date/1,3` | Validate date |
| `iso_week_number/0,1` | ISO 8601 week number |
| `rfc3339_to_system_time/1,2` | Parse RFC3339 → system time |
| `system_time_to_rfc3339/1,2` | System time → RFC3339 string |
| `system_time_to_universal_time/2` | System time to datetime |

```erlang
calendar:local_time().  % {{2024,1,15},{10,30,0}}
calendar:universal_time().

%% Difference in seconds
T1 = calendar:datetime_to_gregorian_seconds({{2024,1,1},{0,0,0}}),
T2 = calendar:datetime_to_gregorian_seconds({{2024,1,15},{12,0,0}}),
T2 - T1.  % 1252800 seconds

calendar:day_of_the_week(2024, 1, 15). % 1 = Monday
calendar:is_leap_year(2024).           % true

%% RFC3339
calendar:system_time_to_rfc3339(
  os:system_time(second), [{unit, second}]).
% "2024-01-15T10:30:00+00:00"
```

## 26. `ets` — Erlang Term Storage (In-Memory)

**Category:** ETS / Storage
**App:** stdlib (implemented in erts)

In-memory term storage shared across processes within a node. O(1) average lookup for `set`/`bag` types.

**Table types:** `set` (unique keys), `ordered_set` (sorted, unique), `bag` (duplicate values per key), `duplicate_bag` (full duplicates)

**Functions:**

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `new/2` | Create table |
| `delete/1,2` | Delete table or specific key |
| `delete_all_objects/1` | Clear table |
| `delete_object/2` | Delete specific tuple |
| `insert/2` | Insert tuple(s) |
| `insert_new/2` | Insert only if key absent |
| `lookup/2` | Get all tuples with key |
| `lookup_element/3,4` | Get specific field of matching tuple |
| `member/2` | Key existence test |
| `update_element/3,4` | Update specific field in-place |
| `update_counter/3,4` | Atomic counter increment |
| `select/2,3` | Match with match spec |
| `select_count/2` | Count matches |
| `select_delete/2` | Delete matches |
| `select_replace/2` | Replace matches |
| `match/2,3` | Pattern matching (returns variable bindings) |
| `match_object/2,3` | Return matching objects |
| `match_delete/2` | Delete matching objects |
| `first/1`, `last/1` | First/last key (ordered_set) |
| `next/2`, `prev/2` | Key navigation (ordered_set) |
| `tab2list/1` | All tuples as list |
| `foldl/3`, `foldr/3` | Fold over all tuples |
| `safe_fixtable/2` | Fix table for safe iteration |
| `info/1,2` | Table metadata |
| `rename/2` | Rename table |
| `give_away/3` | Transfer ownership |
| `setopts/2` | Set table options |
| `slot/2` | Direct slot access |
| `tab2file/2,3` | Serialize to file |
| `file2tab/1,2` | Deserialize from file |
| `from_dets/2` | Load from DETS |
| `to_dets/2` | Dump to DETS |
| `fun2ms/1` | Transform fun to match spec (parse transform) |

**Creation options:** `named_table`, `public`/`protected`/`private`, `{keypos, N}`, `{heir, Pid, Data}`, `compressed`, `{read_concurrency, true}`, `{write_concurrency, true}`

```erlang
%% Create and use a set
T = ets:new(my_table, [set, public, named_table]),
ets:insert(T, {alice, 30}),
ets:insert(T, {bob, 25}),
ets:lookup(T, alice),            % [{alice, 30}]
ets:lookup_element(T, alice, 2), % 30
ets:member(T, carol),            % false

%% Atomic counter
ets:insert(T, {counter, 0}),
ets:update_counter(T, counter, 1),  % 1
ets:update_counter(T, counter, 1),  % 2

%% Match spec (using ms_transform)
-include_lib("stdlib/include/ms_transform.hrl").
MS = ets:fun2ms(fun({Name, Age}) when Age > 20 -> Name end),
ets:select(T, MS). % [alice, bob]

%% Ordered set navigation
OT = ets:new(ot, [ordered_set]),
[ets:insert(OT, {N, N*N}) || N <- lists:seq(1,5)],
ets:first(OT),       % 1
ets:next(OT, 3),     % 4
ets:last(OT).        % 5
```

## 28. `mnesia` — Distributed Database

**Category:** ETS / Storage / Distribution
**App:** mnesia

Distributed, fault-tolerant, in-memory/disk DBMS with transactions. Records are Erlang tuples. Tables can be replicated across nodes.

**Key functions:**

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `start/0`, `stop/0` | Start/stop Mnesia |
| `create_schema/1` | Initialize schema on nodes |
| `delete_schema/1` | Remove schema |
| `create_table/2` | Create table with attributes |
| `delete_table/1` | Delete table |
| `add_table_copy/3` | Add replica on node |
| `transaction/1,3` | Execute fun in transaction |
| `sync_transaction/1,3` | Synchronous transaction |
| `dirty_read/2` | Read without transaction |
| `dirty_write/1` | Write without transaction |
| `dirty_delete/2` | Delete without transaction |
| `read/2,3` | Transactional read |
| `write/1` | Transactional write |
| `delete/3` | Transactional delete |
| `delete_object/1` | Delete specific record |
| `index_read/3` | Read by secondary index |
| `match_object/1,3` | Pattern-match read |
| `select/2,4` | Match spec query |
| `foldl/3,4` | Fold over table |
| `all_keys/1` | All keys in table |
| `first/1`, `last/1`, `next/2`, `prev/2` | Key traversal |
| `table/1,2` | QLC table handle |
| `wait_for_tables/2` | Wait for tables to load |
| `change_table_copy_type/3` | Change `ram_copies`/`disc_copies`/`disc_only_copies` |
| `info/0,1` | System information |
| `system_info/1` | Specific system info |
| `subscribe/1` | Subscribe to table events |
| `activity/2,4` | Run activity in context |

```erlang
%% Define record
-record(person, {name, age, email}).

%% Setup
mnesia:create_schema([node()]),
mnesia:start(),
mnesia:create_table(person, [
  {attributes, record_info(fields, person)},
  {disc_copies, [node()]}
]),

%% Transactional write/read
mnesia:transaction(fun() ->
  mnesia:write(#person{name=alice, age=30, email="alice@example.com"}),
  mnesia:read(person, alice)
end).
% {atomic, [{person, alice, 30, "alice@example.com"}]}
```

```erlang
crypto:hash(sha256, <<"hello">>).
crypto:mac(hmac, sha256, <<"key">>, <<"message">>).

Key = crypto:strong_rand_bytes(32),
IV  = crypto:strong_rand_bytes(12),
{Ciphertext, Tag} = crypto:crypto_one_time_aead(
  aes_256_gcm, Key, IV, <<"plaintext">>, <<"aad">>, true),
crypto:crypto_one_time_aead(
  aes_256_gcm, Key, IV, Ciphertext, <<"aad">>, Tag, false).

{Pub, Priv} = crypto:generate_key(rsa, {2048, 65537}),
Sig = crypto:sign(rsa, sha256, <<"data">>, Priv),
crypto:verify(rsa, sha256, <<"data">>, Sig, Pub).
```

## 41. `gen_server` — Generic Server Behaviour

**Category:** OTP Behaviours
**App:** stdlib

**Callbacks required:** `init/1`, `handle_call/3`, `handle_cast/2`, `handle_info/2`, `terminate/2`, `code_change/3`

| Function | Description |
|---|---|
| `start/3,4` | Start unlinked |
| `start_link/3,4` | Start linked (usual in supervisors) |
| `start_monitor/3,4` | Start + monitor |
| `stop/1,2,3` | Stop server |
| `call/2,3` | Synchronous request |
| `cast/2` | Asynchronous message |
| `multi_call/2,3,4` | Synchronous call to multiple servers |
| `abcast/2,3` | Async cast to multiple servers |
| `reply/2` | Send reply from `handle_call` |
| `enter_loop/3,4,5,6` | Enter gen_server loop from existing process |

```erlang
-module(counter).
-behaviour(gen_server).
-export([start_link/0, increment/1, get/1]).
-export([init/1, handle_call/3, handle_cast/2, handle_info/2,
         terminate/2, code_change/3]).

start_link() -> gen_server:start_link({local, ?MODULE}, ?MODULE, 0, []).
increment(N) -> gen_server:cast(?MODULE, {increment, N}).
get()        -> gen_server:call(?MODULE, get).

init(Init)                     -> {ok, Init}.
handle_call(get, _From, State) -> {reply, State, State}.
handle_cast({increment, N}, State) -> {noreply, State + N}.
handle_info(_Msg, State)       -> {noreply, State}.
terminate(_Reason, _State)     -> ok.
code_change(_OldVsn, State, _Extra) -> {ok, State}.
```

## 42. `gen_statem` — Generic State Machine

**Category:** OTP Behaviours
**App:** stdlib (since OTP 19, replaces gen_fsm)

**Callbacks required:** `callback_mode/0`, `init/1`, state handlers or `handle_event/4`, optionally `terminate/3`, `code_change/4`, `format_status/1`

**Key API:** `start/3,4`, `start_link/3,4`, `start_monitor/3,4`, `stop/1,2,3`, `call/2,3`, `cast/2`, `send_request/2,3`, `receive_response/1,2`

**Callback return actions:** `{next_state, State, Data}`, `{keep_state, Data}`, `{keep_state_and_data}`, `{repeat_state, Data}`, `{stop, Reason}`, `{reply, From, Reply}`, `{next_event, Type, Event}`, `{postpone}`, `{timeout, T, Msg}`, `{state_timeout, T, Msg}`, `{hibernate}`

```erlang
-module(lock).
-behaviour(gen_statem).
-export([start_link/1, push/1]).
-export([callback_mode/0, init/1, locked/3, open/3]).

start_link(Code) -> gen_statem:start_link({local,?MODULE}, ?MODULE, Code, []).
push(Button)     -> gen_statem:cast(?MODULE, {push, Button}).

callback_mode() -> state_functions.
init(Code) -> {ok, locked, #{code => Code, acc => []}}.

locked(cast, {push, Button}, #{code := Code, acc := Acc} = Data) ->
  NewAcc = Acc ++ [Button],
  case lists:suffix(Code, NewAcc) of
    true  -> {next_state, open,   Data#{acc := []}, [{state_timeout, 10000, lock}]};
    false -> {keep_state, Data#{acc := NewAcc}}
  end.

open(state_timeout, lock, Data) -> {next_state, locked, Data};
open(cast, {push, _}, Data)     -> {keep_state, Data}.
```

```erlang
-module(my_sup).
-behaviour(supervisor).
-export([start_link/0, init/1]).

start_link() -> supervisor:start_link({local, ?MODULE}, ?MODULE, []).

init([]) ->
  SupFlags = #{strategy => one_for_one, intensity => 5, period => 10},
  ChildSpec = #{
    id       => my_worker,
    start    => {my_worker, start_link, []},
    restart  => permanent,
    shutdown => 5000,
    type     => worker,
    modules  => [my_worker]
  },
  {ok, {SupFlags, [ChildSpec]}}.
```

## Part 1: Erlang Standard Library

### Group 1: Collections

---

#### `lists` — Singly-Linked List Processing

The most-used module in Erlang. All functions are pure. Lists are singly-linked, so prepend is O(1) and append is O(N).

```erlang
lists:map(fun(X) -> X * 2 end, [1,2,3]).               % [2,4,6]
lists:filter(fun(X) -> X rem 2 =:= 0 end, [1..5]).     % [2,4]
lists:foldl(fun(X, Acc) -> X + Acc end, 0, [1,2,3]).   % 6
lists:partition(fun(X) -> X > 3 end, [1,2,3,4,5]).     % {[4,5],[1,2,3]}
lists:zip([1,2,3], [a,b,c]).                            % [{1,a},{2,b},{3,c}]
lists:enumerate([a,b,c]).                               % [{1,a},{2,b},{3,c}]
lists:uniq([1,2,1,3,2]).                                % [1,2,3]
lists:keysort(2, [{a,3},{b,1},{c,2}]).                  % [{b,1},{c,2},{a,3}]
lists:seq(1, 10, 2).                                    % [1,3,5,7,9]
lists:flatmap(fun(X) -> [X, X*2] end, [1,2,3]).        % [1,2,2,4,3,6]
lists:mapfoldl(fun(X, Acc) -> {X*2, Acc+X} end, 0, [1,2,3]).
% {[2,4,6], 6}
```

Full function inventory (grouped):

| Category | Functions |
|---|---|
| Transform | `map/2`, `filtermap/2`, `flatmap/2`, `mapfoldl/3`, `mapfoldr/3` |
| Filter | `filter/2`, `partition/2`, `takewhile/2`, `dropwhile/2` |
| Fold | `foldl/3`, `foldr/3` |
| Search | `member/2`, `search/2`, `any/2`, `all/2`, `keyfind/3`, `keymember/3`, `keysearch/3` |
| Sort | `sort/1,2`, `usort/1,2`, `keysort/2`, `ukeysort/2`, `merge/1,2,3`, `keymerge/3` |
| Slice | `nth/2`, `nthtail/2`, `sublist/2,3`, `split/2`, `splitwith/2`, `droplast/1` |
| Build | `seq/2,3`, `duplicate/2`, `zip/2,3`, `zipwith/3`, `enumerate/1,2,3`, `join/2`, `append/1,2` |
| Unpack | `unzip/1`, `unzip3/1`, `flatten/1,2`, `last/1`, `reverse/1,2` |
| Aggregate | `sum/1`, `max/1`, `min/1`, `foldl/3` |
| Key-tuple ops | `keydelete/3`, `keyreplace/4`, `keystore/4`, `keytake/3`, `keymap/3` |
| Dedup | `uniq/1,2`, `usort/1,2`, `ukeysort/2`, `umerge/1,2,3` |
| Set-like | `subtract/2`, `prefix/2`, `suffix/2` |
| Side effects | `foreach/2` |

---

#### `maps` — Hash Map (Primary Key-Value Store)

Implemented as HAMT. O(1) average. Keys compared with `=:=` (strict). Default since OTP 17; prefer over `dict`.

```erlang
M = #{name => alice, age => 30},
maps:get(name, M),                                    % alice
maps:get(missing, M, default),                        % default
maps:find(name, M),                                   % {ok, alice}
maps:put(email, "alice@example.com", M),
maps:update_with(age, fun(V) -> V + 1 end, M),
maps:remove(age, M),
maps:filter(fun(_K, V) -> is_integer(V) end, M),
maps:map(fun(_K, V) -> V end, M),
maps:fold(fun(K, V, Acc) -> [{K,V}|Acc] end, [], M),
maps:merge(M, #{city => london}),
maps:with([name], M),                                 % #{name => alice}
maps:without([age], M),
maps:to_list(M),
maps:from_list([{a,1},{b,2}]),
maps:groups_from_list(fun(X) -> X rem 2 end, [1,2,3,4,5]).
% #{0 => [2,4], 1 => [1,3,5]}
```

| Category | Functions |
|---|---|
| Read | `get/2,3`, `find/2`, `is_key/2`, `keys/1`, `values/1`, `size/1` |
| Write | `put/3`, `update/3`, `update_with/3,4`, `remove/2`, `take/2` |
| Bulk | `merge/2`, `merge_with/3`, `intersect/2`, `intersect_with/3`, `with/2`, `without/2` |
| Transform | `map/2`, `filter/2`, `filtermap/2`, `fold/3`, `foreach/2` |
| Convert | `to_list/1`, `from_list/1`, `from_keys/2`, `groups_from_list/2,3` |
| Iterate | `iterator/1,2`, `next/1` |

---

#### `sets` / `ordsets` / `gb_sets` — Set Types

Three implementations with the same logical interface but different performance characteristics.

| Module | Backing | Key comparison | Ordered? | Lookup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sets` | HAMT (v2) | `=:=` | No | O(1) avg |
| `ordsets` | Sorted list | `==` | Yes | O(N) |
| `gb_sets` | AVL tree | `==` | Yes | O(log N) |

```erlang
%% sets — fast, unordered
S = sets:from_list([3,1,4,1,5]),
sets:to_list(sets:union(S, sets:from_list([6,7]))),

%% ordsets — sorted list, numeric coercion in equality
ordsets:to_list(ordsets:from_list([3,1,4,1,5])), % [1,3,4,5]

%% gb_sets — ordered, range queries
G = gb_sets:from_list([5,3,8,1,9]),
gb_sets:smallest(G),    % 1
gb_sets:largest(G),     % 9
I = gb_sets:iterator_from(4, G),
gb_sets:next(I).        % {5, ...}
```

Common interface: `new/0`, `add_element/2`, `del_element/2`, `is_element/2`, `is_empty/1`, `size/1`, `union/1,2`, `intersection/1,2`, `subtract/2`, `is_subset/2`, `is_disjoint/2`, `from_list/1`, `to_list/1`, `filter/2`, `map/2`, `fold/3`

---

#### `gb_trees` — Ordered Key-Value Store

AVL tree map. O(log N) all ops. Keys compared by term order (`<`). Best when you need sorted keys or range iteration.

```erlang
T = gb_trees:from_orddict([{a,1},{b,2},{c,3}]),
gb_trees:get(b, T),        % 2
gb_trees:to_list(T),       % [{a,1},{b,2},{c,3}]
gb_trees:smallest(T),      % {a,1}
gb_trees:largest(T),       % {c,3}
```

---

#### `queue` — Double-Ended FIFO Queue

Amortized O(1) enqueue and dequeue from both ends.

```erlang
Q = queue:from_list([1,2,3,4,5]),
{{value, 1}, Q2} = queue:out(Q),
{{value, 5}, Q3} = queue:out_r(Q),
queue:in(6, Q),
queue:peek(Q).  % {value, 1}
```

---

#### `array` — Sparse Functional Array

O(log N) access. Supports sparse indices with a default value.

```erlang
A = array:new([{default, 0}]),
A2 = array:set(1000, value, A),
array:sparse_to_orddict(A2).  % [{1000, value}]
```

---

#### `proplists` — Property/Option Lists

Used extensively in OTP APIs for option lists. Keys can be atoms (bare) or `{Key, Value}` tuples.

```erlang
Opts = [{debug, true}, {timeout, 5000}, verbose],
proplists:get_value(timeout, Opts),             % 5000
proplists:get_value(missing, Opts, default),    % default
proplists:is_defined(verbose, Opts).            % true
```

---

### Group 2: String and Binary

---

#### `string` — Unicode String Processing

Handles both string/0 (codepoint list) and binary/0. Grapheme-cluster aware.

```erlang
string:length("héllo"),              % 5 (grapheme clusters)
string:to_upper("héllo"),            % "HÉLLO"
string:split("a,b,,c", ",", all),   % ["a","b","","c"]
string:trim("  hello  "),            % "hello"
string:find("hello world", "world"), % "world"
string:pad("hi", 10),               % "hi        "
string:jaro_similarity("kitten", "sitting"). % ~0.746
```

---

#### `binary` — Binary Data

Low-level, efficient due to binary sharing.

```erlang
binary:split(<<"hello world">>, <<" ">>),       % [<<"hello">>,<<"world">>]
binary:match(<<"hello world">>, <<"world">>),   % {6,5}
binary:part(<<"hello world">>, 6, 5),           % <<"world">>
binary:replace(<<"hello">>, <<"hello">>, <<"bye">>),
binary:encode_unsigned(1024),                   % <<4,0>>
```

---

#### `unicode` — Encoding Conversion

```erlang
unicode:characters_to_binary("héllo"),          % <<"héllo"/utf8>>
unicode:characters_to_list(<<"héllo"/utf8>>),   % [104,233,108,108,111]
```

---

#### `io_lib` — String Formatting

Used to build formatted strings without printing them. Returns iolists.

```erlang
Str = lists:flatten(io_lib:format("Value: ~p~n", [{a, b, c}])),
io_lib:fread("~d-~d-~d", "2024-01-15").  % {ok,[2024,1,15],""}
```

---

#### `re` — Regular Expressions (PCRE)

```erlang
{ok, RE} = re:compile("(\\w+)@(\\w+)"),
re:run("user@host", RE, [{capture, all, list}]),
% {match, ["user@host","user","host"]}
```

### Group 6: ETS / Storage

---

#### `ets` — In-Memory Term Storage

Shared across processes on the same node. O(1) average for `set`/`bag`.

Table types: `set`, `ordered_set`, `bag`, `duplicate_bag`

```erlang
T = ets:new(cache, [set, public, named_table]),
ets:insert(T, {alice, 30}),
ets:lookup(T, alice),               % [{alice,30}]
ets:lookup_element(T, alice, 2),    % 30
ets:update_counter(T, counter, 1),  % atomic increment
ets:first(T), ets:next(T, alice),
ets:tab2list(T),
ets:select(T, MatchSpec),
ets:info(T).
```

Creation options: `named_table`, `public`/`protected`/`private`, `{keypos, N}`, `{heir, Pid, Data}`, `compressed`, `{read_concurrency, true}`, `{write_concurrency, true}`

#### `dets` — Disk-Based Term Storage

ETS-compatible API but persistent. Max 2GB per file.

```erlang

```

Transactions, replication, in-memory/disk tables.

```erlang
                              {disc_copies, [node()]}]),

  mnesia:write(#person{name=alice, age=30}),
  mnesia:read(person, alice)
end).
```

Near-zero read cost (no copying). Writing is expensive (triggers GC scan).

## Part 2: Kotlin Standard Library

### Group 1: Collections

---

#### `kotlin.collections` — Core Collection Types

Kotlin has immutable read-only interfaces and mutable counterparts.

| Type | Read-only | Mutable |
|---|---|---|
| Ordered | `List<T>` | `MutableList<T>` |
| Unordered | `Set<T>` | `MutableSet<T>` |
| Key-Value | `Map<K,V>` | `MutableMap<K,V>` |

```kotlin
// Creation
val list = listOf(1, 2, 3)
val mList = mutableListOf(1, 2, 3)
val map = mapOf("a" to 1, "b" to 2)
val mMap = mutableMapOf("a" to 1)
val set = setOf(1, 2, 3)
val array = arrayOf(1, 2, 3)

// Concrete implementations
val linked = LinkedHashMap<String, Int>()    // insertion-ordered
val sorted = TreeMap<String, Int>()          // sorted
val hash = HashMap<String, Int>()            // hash, no order
```

**Transform extensions:**

```kotlin
listOf(1,2,3).map { it * 2 }               // [2,4,6]
listOf(1,2,3).flatMap { listOf(it, it*2) } // [1,2,2,4,3,6]
listOf(1,2,3,4).filter { it % 2 == 0 }    // [2,4]
listOf(1,2,3).mapNotNull { if(it>1) it else null } // [2,3]
listOf(listOf(1,2), listOf(3,4)).flatten() // [1,2,3,4]
```

**Fold/Reduce:**

```kotlin
listOf(1,2,3,4,5).fold(0) { acc, x -> acc + x }    // 15
listOf(1,2,3).reduce { acc, x -> acc + x }           // 6
listOf(1,2,3).runningFold(0) { acc, x -> acc + x }  // [0,1,3,6]
listOf(1,2,3).scan(0) { acc, x -> acc + x }         // [0,1,3,6]
```

**Grouping and partitioning:**

```kotlin
listOf(1,2,3,4,5).groupBy { it % 2 }        // {1:[1,3,5], 0:[2,4]}
listOf(1,2,3,4,5).partition { it > 3 }      // ([4,5], [1,2,3])
listOf(1,2,3,4,5).chunked(2)                // [[1,2],[3,4],[5]]
listOf(1,2,3,4,5).windowed(3)               // [[1,2,3],[2,3,4],[3,4,5]]
listOf(1,2,3,4,5).windowed(3, step=2)       // [[1,2,3],[3,4,5]]
listOf(1,2,3).associate { it to it*it }     // {1:1, 2:4, 3:9}
listOf("a","ab","b").groupingBy { it[0] }.eachCount() // {a:2, b:1}
```

**Search:**

```kotlin
listOf(1,2,3).any { it > 2 }               // true
listOf(1,2,3).all { it > 0 }               // true
listOf(1,2,3).none { it > 5 }              // true
listOf(1,2,3).count { it > 1 }             // 2
listOf(1,2,3).find { it > 1 }              // 2
listOf(1,2,3).findLast { it > 1 }          // 3
listOf(1,2,3).first { it > 1 }             // 2  (throws if not found)
listOf(1,2,3).firstOrNull { it > 5 }       // null
listOf(1,2,3).indexOf(2)                   // 1
listOf(1,2,3).contains(2)                  // true (also: 2 in list)
```

**Aggregation:**

```kotlin
listOf(1,2,3,4,5).sum()                    // 15
listOf(1,2,3,4,5).average()               // 3.0
listOf(1,2,3).minOrNull()                  // 1
listOf(1,2,3).maxOrNull()                  // 3
listOf(1,2,3).minByOrNull { -it }          // 3
listOf(1,2,3).sumOf { it * 2 }            // 12
```

**Sorting:**

```kotlin
listOf(3,1,2).sorted()                     // [1,2,3]
listOf(3,1,2).sortedDescending()           // [3,2,1]
listOf("banana","apple","cherry").sortedBy { it.length }
listOf(1,2,3).sortedByDescending { it }
```

**Slice/Take/Drop:**

```kotlin
listOf(1,2,3,4,5).take(3)                 // [1,2,3]
listOf(1,2,3,4,5).drop(3)                 // [4,5]
listOf(1,2,3,4,5).takeLast(2)             // [4,5]
listOf(1,2,3,4,5).dropLast(2)             // [1,2,3]
listOf(1,2,3,4,5).takeWhile { it < 4 }   // [1,2,3]
listOf(1,2,3,4,5).dropWhile { it < 4 }   // [4,5]
listOf(1,2,3,4,5).slice(1..3)            // [2,3,4]
```

**Zip/Unzip:**

```kotlin
listOf(1,2,3).zip(listOf("a","b","c"))    // [(1,a),(2,b),(3,c)]
listOf(1,2,3).zipWithNext()               // [(1,2),(2,3)]
listOf(1,2,3).zip(listOf("a","b","c")) { a, b -> "$a$b" } // ["1a","2b","3c"]
listOf(Pair(1,"a"), Pair(2,"b")).unzip()  // ([1,2], ["a","b"])
```

**Dedup/Distinct:**

```kotlin
listOf(1,2,1,3,2).distinct()             // [1,2,3]
listOf("abc","ab","bc").distinctBy { it.length } // ["abc","ab"]
```

**Map operations:**

```kotlin
val m = mapOf("a" to 1, "b" to 2)
m["a"]                                    // 1
m.getOrDefault("c", 0)                   // 0
m.getOrElse("c") { 0 }                   // 0
m.filter { (k, v) -> v > 1 }            // {b:2}
m.mapValues { (_, v) -> v * 2 }         // {a:2, b:4}
m.mapKeys { (k, _) -> k.uppercase() }   // {A:1, B:2}
m.entries, m.keys, m.values
m + ("c" to 3)                           // {a:1, b:2, c:3}
m - "a"                                  // {b:2}
```

---

#### `kotlin.sequences` — Lazy Sequences

Sequences are lazy — operations are only evaluated when a terminal op is called. Critical for large/infinite data.

```kotlin
// From collection
listOf(1,2,3).asSequence()

// Generate
generateSequence(1) { it + 1 }          // infinite: 1,2,3,4,...
generateSequence(1) { if (it < 10) it + 1 else null }  // finite

// Builder (suspending-style)
val seq = sequence {
    yield(1)
    yieldAll(listOf(2, 3))
    yield(4)
}

// Fibonacci (infinite)
val fib = generateSequence(Pair(0, 1)) { (a, b) -> Pair(b, a + b) }
    .map { it.first }

// Lazy pipeline (nothing executes until terminal)
(1..1_000_000).asSequence()
    .filter { it % 2 == 0 }
    .map { it * it }
    .take(5)
    .toList()                            // [4,16,36,64,100]
```

Sequences have the same extension functions as collections but evaluated lazily.

---

### Group 2: Scope Functions

These are one of Kotlin's most important DX features. They change the context (`this`/`it`) of a lambda.

| Function | Receiver | Returns | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `let` | `it` (arg) | lambda result | Transform or null-check |
| `run` | `this` | lambda result | Object config + result |
| `with` | `this` (not extension) | lambda result | Multiple ops on object |
| `apply` | `this` | receiver | Object construction/config |
| `also` | `it` (arg) | receiver | Side effects (logging, debug) |

```kotlin
// let — transform or null-guard
val name: String? = "Alice"
val length = name?.let { it.length }          // 5 or null

val result = listOf(1,2,3).let {
    it.filter { n -> n > 1 }.sum()            // 5
}

// run — configure + produce result
val config = run {
    val base = 10
    val multiplier = 3
    base * multiplier                          // 30
}

// with — multiple ops, named receiver
val sb = with(StringBuilder()) {
    append("Hello")
    append(", ")
    append("World")
    toString()                                 // "Hello, World"
}

// apply — builder pattern, returns self
val person = Person().apply {
    name = "Alice"
    age = 30
    email = "alice@example.com"
}                                              // returns Person

// also — side effect, returns original
val numbers = mutableListOf(1, 2, 3)
    .also { println("Before: $it") }
    .also { it.add(4) }
    .also { println("After: $it") }           // returns the list
```

**`takeIf` and `takeUnless`:**

```kotlin
val n = 42
n.takeIf { it > 0 }                          // 42
n.takeIf { it > 100 }                        // null
n.takeUnless { it > 100 }                    // 42
n.takeUnless { it > 0 }                      // null

// Common pattern
val validated = input.takeIf { it.isNotBlank() }
    ?: throw IllegalArgumentException("blank")
```

### Group 3: Text

---

#### `kotlin.text` — String Extensions

```kotlin
// Check
"hello".isEmpty()                            // false
"  ".isBlank()                               // true
"hello world".contains("world")              // true
"hello".startsWith("hel")                    // true
"hello".endsWith("llo")                      // true
"hello".matches(Regex("h.*o"))               // true

// Transform
"hello".uppercase()                          // "HELLO"
"hello".capitalize()                         // "Hello" (deprecated; use replaceFirstChar)
"hello world".split(" ")                     // ["hello","world"]
"  hello  ".trim()                           // "hello"
"  hello  ".trimStart()                      // "hello  "
"hello".padStart(10)                         // "     hello"
"hello".padEnd(10, '.')                      // "hello....."
"hello".reversed()                           // "olleh"
"ha".repeat(3)                               // "hahaha"
"hello world".replace("world", "there")      // "hello there"
"hello world".replaceFirst("l", "L")        // "heLlo world"

// Extract
"hello"[1]                                   // 'e'
"hello world".substring(6)                   // "world"
"hello world".substringBefore(" ")          // "hello"
"hello world".substringAfter(" ")           // "world"
"hello world".substringAfterLast("l")       // "d"
"hello".take(3)                              // "hel"
"hello".drop(3)                              // "lo"
"hello".first()                              // 'h'
"hello".last()                               // 'o'

// Convert
"42".toInt()                                 // 42
"42".toIntOrNull()                           // 42
"abc".toIntOrNull()                          // null
"3.14".toDouble()                            // 3.14
"hello".toCharArray()                        // CharArray

// Build
buildString {
    append("Hello")
    appendLine(", World")
    repeat(3) { append("!") }
}
```

#### `Regex`

```kotlin
val re = Regex("(\\w+)@(\\w+\\.\\w+)")
re.matches("user@host.com")                  // true
re.find("email: user@host.com")?.value      // "user@host.com"
re.findAll("a@b.c d@e.f").map { it.value }.toList()
re.replace("hello world", "X")
re.split("a,b,,c")                          // ["a","b","","c"]

// Groups
val m = re.find("user@host.com")
m?.groupValues                               // ["user@host.com","user","host.com"]
m?.groups?.get(1)?.value                    // "user"
```

### Group 6: Result and Error Handling

---

#### `kotlin.Result` / `runCatching`

```kotlin
// Wrap any operation
val result: Result<Int> = runCatching { "42".toInt() }
val fail:   Result<Int> = runCatching { "abc".toInt() }

result.isSuccess                             // true
result.isFailure                             // false
result.getOrNull()                           // 42
result.getOrDefault(0)                       // 42
result.getOrElse { 0 }                      // 42
result.getOrThrow()                          // 42

fail.exceptionOrNull()                       // NumberFormatException

result.map { it * 2 }                       // Result(84)
result.mapCatching { it / 0 }              // Result(failure)
result.flatMap { runCatching { it * 2 } }
result.recover { 0 }                        // Result(42) if ok, Result(0) if fail
result.recoverCatching { 0 }

result.onSuccess { println("Got: $it") }
result.onFailure { println("Error: $it") }

// Fold
result.fold(
    onSuccess = { "ok: $it" },
    onFailure = { "err: ${it.message}" }
)
```

```kotlin
import kotlin.time.*

val d1 = 5.seconds
```

### Group 8: Coroutines (`kotlinx.coroutines`)

#### Core builders and scope

```kotlin
// Launch (fire and forget, returns Job)
val job = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Default).launch {
    delay(1000)
    println("done")
}

// Async (returns Deferred<T>)
val deferred = CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).async {
    fetchFromNetwork()
}
val result = deferred.await()

// Structured concurrency
coroutineScope {
    val a = async { computeA() }
    val b = async { computeB() }
    a.await() + b.await()           // both run concurrently
}

supervisorScope {
    val a = async { mayFail() }
    val b = async { alsoMayFail() }
    // one failure doesn't cancel the other
}

// withContext (switch dispatcher)
withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { readFile() }
withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { heavyCompute() }

// Timeout
withTimeout(5000) { slowOperation() }       // throws on timeout
withTimeoutOrNull(5000) { slowOperation() } // null on timeout
```

---

#### Dispatchers

| Dispatcher | Use |
|---|---|
| `Dispatchers.Default` | CPU-bound work (thread pool = CPU count) |
| `Dispatchers.IO` | Blocking I/O (expandable pool, up to 64) |
| `Dispatchers.Main` | UI thread (Android/JavaFX/Swing) |
| `Dispatchers.Unconfined` | No thread affinity (use carefully) |

---

#### Flow — Reactive Streams

```kotlin
// Cold flow (executes per collector)
val flow: Flow<Int> = flow {
    emit(1)
    delay(100)
    emit(2)
    emit(3)
}

// Collect
flow.collect { println(it) }

// Operators
flow
    .filter { it > 1 }
    .map { it * 2 }
    .take(2)
    .collect { println(it) }

// Terminal operators
flow.toList()
flow.first()
flow.fold(0) { acc, v -> acc + v }

// StateFlow (hot, always has a value)
val state = MutableStateFlow(0)
state.value = 1
state.collect { /* always gets current + updates */ }

// SharedFlow (hot, broadcast)
val shared = MutableSharedFlow<Int>(replay = 1)
shared.emit(42)
shared.collect { }

// Combining
combine(flow1, flow2) { a, b -> a + b }
zip(flow1, flow2) { a, b -> Pair(a, b) }
merge(flow1, flow2)
flow.flatMapLatest { ... }
flow.debounce(300)
flow.sample(1000)
flow.buffer()
flow.conflate()
flow.flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)
```

---

#### Channel — Communication Between Coroutines

```kotlin
val channel = Channel<Int>(capacity = 10)

launch { channel.send(1); channel.send(2); channel.close() }
launch { for (v in channel) println(v) }

// Produce
val ch = produce { (1..5).forEach { send(it) } }

// Actors pattern
val actor = actor<Int> {
    for (msg in channel) process(msg)
}
```

---

#### Mutex and Semaphore

```kotlin
val mutex = Mutex()
mutex.withLock { sharedState++ }

val semaphore = Semaphore(permits = 3)
semaphore.withPermit { accessResource() }
```

---

### Group 9: Reflection

---

#### `kotlin.reflect`

```kotlin
val klass: KClass<String> = String::class
klass.simpleName                             // "String"
klass.qualifiedName                          // "kotlin.String"
klass.isData                                 // false
klass.constructors
klass.members
klass.memberFunctions
klass.memberProperties

val prop = Person::name                      // KProperty1<Person, String>
prop.get(person)                             // "Alice"

val func = String::length                    // KProperty1<String, Int>
func.get("hello")                            // 5

// Callable references
val ref: (String) -> Int = String::length
listOf("hello", "world").map(String::length) // [5,5]

// Type check
person::class == Person::class
person is Person
```

## Part 3: Mapping Strategies — Stdlib Design for KorE

---

### 3.1 The Collections API

**The problem:** Erlang's collections are module-prefixed (`lists:map`, `maps:get`). Kotlin's are method-chained extensions (`list.map { }`). These are fundamentally different invocation styles.

**Option A — Pure Kotlin Method Chain (Recommended)**

Expose all collections as KorE types with chainable extension functions. The BEAM native types (list, map, binary) are wrapped at the language boundary.

```kore
// All operations are extensions on the collection type
val evens = listOf(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
    .filter { it % 2 == 0 }
    .map { it * it }
    .sorted()

val grouped = users
    .groupBy { it.role }
    .mapValues { it.sortedBy { u -> u.name } }
```

This compiles down to `lists:filter`, `lists:map`, `lists:sort` etc. The developer never sees the Erlang module names. This is exactly what Elixir does with the `Enum` module — a single namespace for all collection operations.

Pros: Familiar to Kotlin/Java devs. Clean business logic. IDE-friendly.
Cons: Wrapper overhead (minimal on BEAM due to binary sharing). Hides BEAM idioms from new learners.

---

**Option B — Dual API (Functional + Chained)**

Expose both styles. Module-style for performance-critical/low-level code, chain-style for business logic.

```kore
// Chain style (default)
users.filter { it.active }.map { it.name }

// Module style (explicit, for when you need it)
Lists.filter(users) { it.active }
Maps.merge(m1, m2)
```

This is how Elixir works — `Enum.map` is the explicit style; pipe operator `|>` provides chaining. Gleam does the same.

Pros: Gives power users access to raw module semantics.
Cons: Two ways to do the same thing can split codebases.

---

**Option C — Pipe Operator as Primary Chaining Mechanism**

Instead of Kotlin's dot-chain, use a `|>` pipe operator as the canonical way to chain. Feels more BEAM-native.

```kore
users
    |> filter { it.active }
    |> map { it.name }
    |> sortedBy { it }
```

This is Elixir and Gleam's approach. It maps directly to Erlang function call chaining.

Pros: BEAM-native feel. No wrapping needed — it's just `lists:filter(lists:map(...))` rewritten left-to-right.
Cons: Less familiar to Kotlin developers. Requires the developer to know which module each function lives in.

---

**My recommendation: Option A as default, Option C as optional syntax sugar.**

Use Kotlin's extension function chain as the primary DX. Implement `|>` as an optional operator (Scala 3 has it, Kotlin doesn't natively). Kotlin developers feel at home; Erlang/Elixir developers get their pipe operator too.

---

### 3.2 Scope Functions — Let, Apply, Also, Run, With

**The problem:** Kotlin's scope functions (`let`, `apply`, `also`, `run`, `with`) are idioms for transforming values, building objects, and adding side effects inline. Erlang has no equivalent — you just bind variables.

**Option A — Keep Kotlin Scope Functions As-Is (Recommended)**

Since KorE has a Kotlin-flavored syntax, `let`, `apply`, `also`, `run`, `with` are first-class. They compile down to immediate function application.

```kore
val connection = DbConnection()
    .apply {
        host = "localhost"
        port = 5432
        timeout = 5000
    }

val result = payload
    .also { logger.debug("Processing: $it") }
    .let { transform(it) }
    .takeIf { it.isValid() }
    ?: throw ValidationError("invalid payload")
```

This is pure syntax — zero BEAM overhead. A `.apply { }` block is just a function that takes a receiver and returns it. `let` is `fun <T, R>(T, (T) -> R): R`. Both compile to trivial BEAM function calls.

---

**Option B — Pipe Operator Instead of Let**

Instead of `.let { }`, use `|>` for transformation and drop the other scope functions.

```kore
payload
    |> tap { logger.debug("Processing: $it") }    // = also
    |> transform(_)
    |> validate(_)
```

The `tap` function (from Ruby/Elixir) does what `also` does: side effect, return original. This is cleaner in a pipe-heavy style.

Pros: Consistent with pipe-first philosophy.
Cons: Loses the distinction between `apply` (builder pattern) and `let` (transform). Enterprise Kotlin devs will miss `apply`.

---

**Option C — Elixir-style with/2 for Error Pipelines**

For error-handling pipelines, Elixir's `with` macro chains operations that return `{:ok, val} | {:error, reason}`. This is different from Kotlin's `with` but extremely powerful for BEAM.

```kore
// KorE with-pipeline (inspired by Elixir's with)
val result = with {
    val user  <- findUser(userId)        // unwraps Result<User>
    val order <- createOrder(user)       // unwraps Result<Order>
    val _     <- sendConfirmation(order) // unwraps Result<Unit>
    order
} catch {
    UserNotFound -> handleMissing()
    OrderFailed  -> handleOrderError()
}
```

This is the most powerful option for business logic that involves multiple steps that can each fail.

Pros: Natural error handling for BEAM-style code. Eliminates nested `if/else` or `try/catch` chains.
Cons: Introduces new semantics that Kotlin developers don't know. Requires a new mental model.

---

**My recommendation: Keep all five Kotlin scope functions (Option A). Additionally provide `with`-pipeline (Option C) as a separate, named construct (perhaps `pipeline { }` to avoid name conflict with Kotlin's `with`). Do not replace scope functions with pipes — both can coexist.**

---

### 3.3 Functional Chaining — Map, Filter, Fold

**The problem:** Erlang uses `lists:map(Fun, List)`. Kotlin uses `list.map { }`. KorE must pick a canonical style.

**Option A — Extension Functions on BEAM Types**

`list.map`, `map.filter`, `binary.split` as first-class extension functions on native BEAM types. This is the Elixir approach with more Kotlin syntax.

```kore
val doubled = [1, 2, 3].map { it * 2 }   // compiles to lists:map
val filtered = myMap.filter { _, v -> v > 0 }  // compiles to maps:filter
```

Pros: Simplest for the developer. One way to do things.
Cons: Type-inference heavy. Need to decide: does `[1,2,3]` return a KorE `List` type or an Erlang list?

---

**Option B — Separate KorE Collection Types**

KorE has its own `List<T>`, `Map<K,V>`, `Set<T>` types that wrap BEAM structures and provide the extension API. Interop with raw Erlang is explicit.

```kore
val koreList: List<Int> = listOf(1, 2, 3)  // KorE type
val erlList: ErlList    = erlang.list([1,2,3])  // raw BEAM

koreList.map { it * 2 }         // KorE API
erlList.toList().map { it * 2 } // convert first
```

Pros: Clean type system. No ambiguity.
Cons: Interop with Erlang libraries requires explicit conversion — friction when calling OTP APIs.

---

**Option C — Transparent Unification**

KorE's collection types compile to BEAM native types. `List<T>` IS an Erlang list at runtime. No wrapper. Extension functions are compile-time sugar that emit `lists:*` calls directly.

```kore
val xs: List<Int> = [1, 2, 3]   // this IS an Erlang list
xs.map { it * 2 }               // compiles to: lists:map(fun(X) -> X*2 end, xs)
```

This is the Gleam approach. Zero overhead. Full Erlang interop.

Pros: Zero overhead. Erlang libraries work directly.
Cons: Type system is constrained by what BEAM can represent. Harder to provide Kotlin-specific features like lazy evaluation.

---

**My recommendation: Option C for core collection types (List, Map, Set, Binary), Option A's API surface. Lazy sequences (Kotlin's `Sequence`) map to Erlang generators/comprehensions or a custom lazy list structure. This gives zero-overhead interop with full Kotlin-style API.**

---

### 3.4 Sequences and Lazy Evaluation

**The problem:** Kotlin's `Sequence<T>` is lazy. Erlang has lazy evaluation via generators and list comprehensions, but no standard lazy sequence type.

**Option A — Map Sequence to Erlang Generators**

```kore
// KorE
val fib = generateSequence(Pair(0, 1)) { (a, b) -> Pair(b, a + b) }
    .map { it.first }
    .take(10)
    .toList()
```

Compiles to a recursive function that generates elements on demand. Not a persistent data structure — evaluated once.

---

**Option B — Use Erlang's List Comprehensions**

Expose list comprehensions as a KorE `sequence { }` builder.

```kore
val evens = sequence {
    for (x in 1..100) {
        if (x % 2 == 0) yield(x)
    }
}
// compiles to: [X || X <- lists:seq(1,100), X rem 2 =:= 0]
```

Pros: Direct mapping to native BEAM construct. No overhead.
Cons: Not truly lazy — list comprehensions evaluate eagerly.

---

**Option C — Lazy List as a KorE Primitive**

Implement a proper lazy list type using BEAM processes or closures.

```kore
// Each element is a closure returning {head, tail}
val naturals: LazyList<Int> = lazyList { n -> n } // generates 1,2,3,...
```

Pros: Truly lazy. Can model infinite streams.
Cons: Closure overhead. Not idiomatic BEAM.

---

**My recommendation: Option A for `generateSequence` and finite lazy pipelines (maps to tail-recursive functions). Option B for comprehension-style builders. Don't implement Option C — BEAM already has processes for true streams; use them instead (this bridges to Session 4's Flow/GenStage discussion).**

---

### 3.5 Error Handling — Result vs Exceptions vs Tagged Tuples

**The problem:** Erlang uses `{ok, Value} | {error, Reason}` tagged tuples everywhere. Kotlin uses exceptions and `Result<T>`. These are very different mental models.

**Option A — Kotlin Result<T> as the Surface API**

KorE functions return `Result<T>`. Under the hood, `{ok, V}` becomes `Result.success(V)` and `{error, R}` becomes `Result.failure(reason)`. Erlang OTP functions are automatically wrapped.

```kore
fun readFile(path: String): Result<String> =
    runCatching { File.readFile(path) }  // wraps {ok,_} | {error,_}

readFile("/etc/hostname")
    .map { it.trim() }
    .onSuccess { println("Host: $it") }
    .onFailure { println("Error: $it") }
```

Pros: Familiar to Kotlin developers. Composable with `map`, `flatMap`.
Cons: Hides BEAM's supervisory error philosophy. "Let it crash" becomes unnatural.

---

**Option B — Keep Tagged Tuples, Add Pattern Matching Syntax**

KorE uses BEAM's `{ok, v} | {error, reason}` natively. Pattern matching handles both cases cleanly.

```kore
when (val r = readFile("/etc/hostname")) {
    is Ok  -> println("Host: ${r.value}")
    is Err -> println("Error: ${r.reason}")
}
```

Where `Ok` and `Err` are KorE-defined sealed classes that pattern-match against `{ok, _}` and `{error, _}` tuples transparently.

Pros: Stays true to BEAM. No wrapping overhead. OTP interop is natural.
Cons: Less ergonomic for Kotlin developers who expect `Result`.

---

**Option C — Dual Mode**

Both `Result<T>` and `{ok, _} | {error, _}` are valid. Provide conversion functions.

```kore
val result: Result<String> = readFile(path)  // KorE style
val tagged: OkErr<String>  = readFile(path).toOkErr()  // BEAM style

// Tagged tuple functions work with when:
when (tagged) {
    is Ok  -> tagged.value
    is Err -> tagged.reason
}
```

---

**Option D — Railway-Oriented Programming (Gleam-style)**

Gleam's approach: all functions return `Result(Ok(a), Err(e))`. Pipe operator chains results automatically unwrapping successes and short-circuiting on errors.

```kore
// The |> operator unwraps Ok and short-circuits on Err
val result = validateInput(input)
    |> processPayment(_)
    |> sendConfirmation(_)
    |> logTransaction(_)
```

If any step returns `Err`, the entire chain returns that `Err`. This is `Result.flatMap` chaining with pipe syntax.

Pros: Extremely clean business logic. Explicit about errors. No exceptions.
Cons: New model for both Kotlin and Erlang developers.

---

**My recommendation: Option B as the primary model (`Ok`/`Err` sealed classes over tagged tuples) + Option D's pipeline syntax for chains. This is the most BEAM-aligned choice. Option A's `Result<T>` can be provided as a compatibility adapter for Kotlin library interop. The key insight is: KorE should NOT hide `{ok,_}|{error,_}` — it should embrace it with better syntax.**

---

### 3.6 String and Binary Handling

**The problem:** Erlang has two string representations (char lists and binaries) plus `iolist`. Kotlin has a single `String` type.

**Option A — KorE String = UTF-8 Binary**

`String` in KorE compiles to Erlang `binary()` with UTF-8 encoding. String interpolation compiles to binary construction.

```kore
val name = "Alice"             // <<"Alice">>
val msg = "Hello, $name!"     // <<"Hello, ", Name/binary, "!">>

// Binary operations available on String
name.length                    // string:length(Name)
name.toUpperCase()             // string:to_upper(Name)
name.split(",")               // binary:split(Name, <<",">>)
```

Pros: Single string type. No `iolist` confusion. Efficient.
Cons: Char lists (used by some OTP APIs) require explicit conversion.

---

**Option B — KorE String = Iolist Under the Hood**

`String` is an iolist. Concatenation is O(1) (just wrapping in a list). When an API needs a binary, auto-convert.

```kore
val parts = ["Hello", ", ", "World"]
val msg = parts.joinToString("")   // iolist, not yet a binary
send(msg)                          // auto-converts to binary when needed
```

Pros: Zero-copy string building (huge performance win for large strings).
Cons: Surprise type behavior. Debugging shows iolists, not strings.

---

**Option C — Explicit String vs Binary Types**

```kore
val str: String = "hello"           // char list internally
val bin: Binary = b"hello"          // binary literal
val raw: Iolist = [str, bin, "\n"]  // iolist
```

Pros: Full type precision. No surprises.
Cons: More verbose. Requires developers to think about encoding.

---

**My recommendation: Option A. UTF-8 binary as the universal `String` type. Iolist is available as `Iolist` type for performance-critical string building but not the default. Char lists from legacy OTP APIs are auto-converted at the KorE boundary. This is what Elixir does, and it works well.**

---

### 3.7 The Concurrency Stdlib — Processes, Tasks, Channels

**The problem:** Kotlin's concurrency is coroutines (cooperative, on JVM threads). Erlang's concurrency is lightweight processes with message passing. They are fundamentally different. KorE should expose BEAM's model, not fake coroutines.

**Option A — Expose BEAM Processes Directly**

KorE's `spawn`, `send`, `receive` are thin wrappers over Erlang BIFs with Kotlin-friendly syntax.

```kore
val pid = spawn {
    receive { msg ->
        when (msg) {
            is Stop  -> return@spawn
            is Greet -> println("Hello, ${msg.name}")
        }
    }
}

pid.send(Greet("Alice"))
pid.send(Stop)
```

Pros: Zero abstraction. Full BEAM power. Teaches the BEAM model directly.
Cons: Unfamiliar for Kotlin/JVM developers.

---

**Option B — Coroutine-Like Syntax Mapping to Processes**

Use `async { }` and `await` as syntax sugar over `spawn_monitor` + `receive`.

```kore
val deferred = async {
    computeExpensiveThing()
}
val result = deferred.await()  // compiles to spawn_monitor + receive
```

Pros: Familiar syntax for Kotlin developers.
Cons: Misleading — BEAM async is not cooperative like coroutines. `await` implies thread blocking but on BEAM it's a `receive` that suspends the process, not the thread. Could cause confusion about scheduling.

---

**Option C — Task Abstraction (Elixir-style)**

```kore
val task = Task.async { computeExpensiveThing() }
val result = Task.await(task, timeout = 5.seconds)

// Parallel map
val results = Task.awaitAll(
    Task.async { fetchA() },
    Task.async { fetchB() },
    Task.async { fetchC() }
)
```

This maps directly to Elixir's `Task` module, which wraps `spawn_monitor` + `receive`. Clean, familiar to Elixir users, approachable for Kotlin users.

Pros: Simple abstraction. Direct BEAM mapping. Used in production at scale.
Cons: Still requires understanding message-passing for advanced use.

---

**My recommendation: Option C as the high-level API (`Task.async`/`Task.await`). Option A's raw `spawn`/`send`/`receive` are always available for power users. Option B is explicitly NOT provided — fake coroutine syntax on BEAM is a footgun. Session 4 covers GenServer, which is the real actor abstraction.**

---

### 3.8 Logging

**Option A — Map to Erlang's `logger`**

```kore
Logger.info("Server started on port $port")
Logger.error("Connection failed", mapOf("reason" to reason))
Logger.debug { "Expensive: ${computeDebugInfo()}" }  // lazy
```

Compiles to `logger:info`, `logger:error`. The lambda form for debug compiles to a guard-checked call (no evaluation if level is above debug).

---

**Option B — Structured Logging First**

```kore
log {
    level = Level.INFO
    message = "User authenticated"
    fields {
        userId = user.id
        method = "oauth2"
        duration = elapsed
    }
}
```

Compiles to `logger:info(#{level => info, msg => ..., meta => #{...}})`. Structured logging natively on BEAM's `logger` metadata system.

---

**My recommendation: Option B with Option A as shorthand. Structured logging is the right default for production systems. Short `Logger.info(...)` is acceptable for simple cases but structured maps should be the canonical form.**

---

### Summary Table — Stdlib Mapping Decisions

| Area | Recommended Approach | Key Decision |
|---|---|---|
| Collection API | Kotlin-style extension functions, transparent BEAM types | `list.map { }` → `lists:map` |
| Chaining | Extension chain + optional `\|>` | Both styles valid |
| Scope functions | Keep all 5 Kotlin scope functions | `apply`, `let`, `also`, `run`, `with` |
| Error handling | `Ok`/`Err` sealed classes over tagged tuples | No hiding of BEAM error model |
| Error pipelines | Railway `\|>` short-circuit on `Err` | Explicit `pipeline { }` construct |
| Strings | UTF-8 binary as `String` | Single type, auto-convert from charlists |
| Lazy evaluation | `generateSequence` → tail recursion, `sequence { }` → comprehensions | No fake lazy lists |
| Concurrency | `Task.async`/`Task.await` over BEAM processes | No fake coroutines |
| Logging | Structured `log { }` builder, `Logger.level()` shorthand | BEAM `logger` underneath |
| Math | `kotlin.math` naming, same functions | Direct mapping |
| Time | `kotlin.time.Duration` API, compiles to `erlang:monotonic_time` | No JVM time classes |
| Collections mutability | Read-only by default | Mutable variants are explicit |

---

**Key decisions to make before Session 3:**

1. Do you want `|>` as a first-class operator or just `.let { }`? This affects the entire stdlib design philosophy.
2. `Ok`/`Err` vs `Result<T>` — which should be the canonical error type? My recommendation is `Ok`/`Err`, but this is a values question about how close to BEAM you want to stay.
3. Should `Task.async` timeout be mandatory (Elixir forces it) or optional (Kotlin's `Deferred.await` has no default timeout)? Erlang's "let it crash" philosophy says mandatory — orphaned processes are a bug.
