1636: ---
1637: 
1638: ### How Validation Integrates with PingConn
1639: 
1640: Validation runs as a middleware stage, after body parsing and before the controller is called. The `ValidationMiddleware` is automatically installed when `@Valid` is present on a `@RequestBody` parameter:
1641: 
1642: ```kotlin
1643: // The middleware chain for a validated endpoint:
1644: // 1. JsonParser — parses body, puts in conn.body
1645: // 2. ParameterBinder — binds @RequestBody to CreateUserRequest
1646: // 3. ValidationMiddleware — validates bound object, collects violations
1647: // 4. Controller function — only called if validation passes
1648: 
1649: @Post
1650: fun create(@Valid @RequestBody request: CreateUserRequest): UserResponse { ... }
1651: ```
1652: 
1653: If validation fails, `ValidationMiddleware` halts the pipeline and returns a 422 response with a `ValidationProblemDetail` body. The controller is never called.
1654: 
1655: The compiler generates a validator function for each validated data class:
1656: 
1657: ```kotlin
1658: // Generated by compiler for CreateUserRequest
1659: fun validate(request: CreateUserRequest): List<Violation> = buildList {
1660:     if (request.email.isBlank())
1661:         add(Violation("email", "Email is required"))
1662:     if (!request.email.matches(EMAIL_REGEX))
1663:         add(Violation("email", "Must be a valid email address"))
1664:     if (request.password.isBlank())
1665:         add(Violation("password", "Password is required"))
1666:     if (request.password.length < 8 || request.password.length > 100)
1667:         add(Violation("password", "Password must be 8-100 characters"))
1668:     if (request.name.isBlank())
1669:         add(Violation("name", "Name is required"))
1670:     request.age?.let { age ->
1671:         if (age < 0) add(Violation("age", "must be greater than or equal to 0"))
1672:         if (age > 150) add(Violation("age", "must be less than or equal to 150"))
1673:     }
1674:     request.countryCode?.let { code ->
1675:         if (!code.matches(Regex("[A-Z]{2}")))
1676:             add(Violation("countryCode", "Must be a 2-letter country code"))
1677:     }
1678: }
1679: ```
1680: 
1681: All violations are collected before returning — no fail-fast behavior. The entire list of violations is returned so the client can correct all errors in one round trip.
1682: 
1683: ---
1684: 
1685: ### Custom Validators
1686: 
1687: ```kotlin
1688: // Define the annotation
1689: @Target(AnnotationTarget.FIELD)
1690: @Retention(AnnotationRetention.RUNTIME)
1691: @Constraint(validatedBy = [UniqueEmailValidator::class])
1692: annotation class UniqueEmail(
1693:     val message: String = "Email address is already registered"
1694: )
1695: 
1696: // Implement the validator
1697: class UniqueEmailValidator(
1698:     private val userRepository: UserRepository
1699: ) : ConstraintValidator<UniqueEmail, String> {
1700:     override fun isValid(value: String?, context: ConstraintValidatorContext): Boolean {
1701:         if (value == null) return true  // @NotNull handles nulls
1702:         return when (userRepository.findByEmail(value)) {
1703:             is Ok -> false  // found = not unique
1704:             is Err -> true  // not found = unique
1705:         }
1706:     }
1707: }
1708: 
1709: // Usage
1710: data class CreateUserRequest(
1711:     @field:NotBlank
1712:     @field:Email
1713:     @field:UniqueEmail
1714:     val email: String,
1715:     // ...
1716: )
1717: ```
1718: 
1719: Custom validators that need dependencies (like `UniqueEmailValidator` needing `UserRepository`) are resolved through Ping's DI system. The `@Constraint(validatedBy = ...)` annotation tells the compiler to inject an instance of the validator class, which in turn resolves its dependencies through the normal DI chain.
1720: 
1721: ---
1722: 
1723: ### Type-Level Validation (Refined Types)
1724: 
1725: For cases where validation is a core invariant of the type rather than a request-level check, Ping supports refined types:
1726: 
1727: ```kotlin
1728: // Refined type — construction validates at the point of creation
1729: @Refined
1730: value class Email(val value: String) {
1731:     init {
1732:         require(value.isNotBlank()) { "Email must not be blank" }
1733:         require(value.matches(EMAIL_REGEX)) { "Invalid email format: $value" }
1734:     }
1735: }
1736: 
1737: @Refined
1738: value class PasswordHash private constructor(val hash: String) {
1739:     companion object {
1740:         fun of(plaintext: String): Ok<PasswordHash> | Err<ValidationError> {
1741:             if (plaintext.length < 8) return Err(ValidationError("Password too short"))
1742:             return Ok(PasswordHash(BCrypt.hash(plaintext)))
1743:         }
1744:     }
1745: }
1746: 
1747: // Usage — the type system enforces validity
1748: data class User(
1749:     val id: String,
1750:     val email: Email,  // Can never hold an invalid email
1751:     val passwordHash: PasswordHash
1752: )
1753: ```
1754: 
1755: Refined types are the right tool for domain invariants. `@field:Email` annotations are the right tool for request DTO validation. They solve different problems and should not be conflated.
1756: 
1757: ---
1758: 
1759: ## 10.8 — WebSocket and Channels
1760: 
1761: ### The Channel Model
1762: 
1763: Ping's WebSocket support is built on Phoenix Channels semantics: connections join topics, and events flow bidirectionally within those topics. This is a richer model than bare WebSocket, and it maps naturally to the BEAM's process model.
1764: 
1765: Each WebSocket connection is a dedicated BEAM process — a `Channel` process that is a specialized GenServer. When a client connects, a channel process is spawned and linked to the endpoint supervisor. The channel process handles join/leave/event messages from the client and can send messages back to the client or broadcast to all subscribers of a topic.
1766: 
1767: This is structurally excellent for the BEAM. Tens of thousands of concurrent WebSocket connections means tens of thousands of channel processes. Each is isolated — a misbehaving connection crashes its own process without affecting any other connection.
1768: 
1769: ---
1770: 
1771: ### `@WebSocketController`
1772: 
1773: ```kotlin
1774: @WebSocketController(topic = "notification:{userId}")
1775: class NotificationChannel(
1776:     private val notificationService: NotificationService,
1777:     private val presence: Presence
1778: ) {
1779: 
1780:     @OnConnect
1781:     fun onJoin(
1782:         socket: ChannelSocket,
1783:         params: Map<String, String>
1784:     ): Ok<ChannelState> | Err<String> {
1785:         val userId = socket.assigns["userId"] as? String
1786:             ?: return Err("Unauthorized")
1787: 
1788:         // Track presence
1789:         presence.track(socket, userId, mapOf(
1790:             "online_at" to BEAMTime.now(),
1791:             "device" to params["device"]
1792:         ))
1793: 
1794:         // Send initial state
1795:         socket.push("initial_state", mapOf(
1796:             "unreadCount" to notificationService.unreadCount(userId)
1797:         ))
1798: 
1799:         return Ok(ChannelState(userId = userId))
1800:     }
1801: 
1802:     @OnDisconnect
1803:     fun onLeave(
1804:         socket: ChannelSocket,
1805:         reason: LeaveReason,
1806:         state: ChannelState
1807:     ) {
1808:         Logger.info("User ${state.userId} left notification channel")
1809:         // Presence cleanup is automatic when the process exits
1810:     }
1811: 
1812:     @OnMessage("mark_read")
1813:     fun onMarkRead(
1814:         socket: ChannelSocket,
1815:         payload: MarkReadPayload,
1816:         state: ChannelState
1817:     ): Ok<ChannelState> | Err<String> {
1818:         return when (notificationService.markRead(state.userId, payload.notificationId)) {
1819:             is Ok -> {
1820:                 socket.push("notification_read", mapOf("id" to payload.notificationId))
1821:                 Ok(state)
1822:             }
1823:             is Err -> Err("Failed to mark notification as read")
1824:         }
1825:     }
1826: 
1827:     @OnMessage("mark_all_read")
1828:     fun onMarkAllRead(
1829:         socket: ChannelSocket,
1830:         payload: EmptyPayload,
1831:         state: ChannelState
1832:     ): Ok<ChannelState> | Err<String> {
1833:         notificationService.markAllRead(state.userId)
1834:         socket.push("all_notifications_read", emptyMap())
1835:         return Ok(state)
1836:     }
1837: }
1838: ```
1839: 
1840: **The `topic` parameter** supports pattern matching: `"notification:{userId}"` means this channel handles any topic matching that pattern. The `{userId}` segment is extracted and available in `socket.topic_params["userId"]`.
1841: 
1842: **What the compiler generates:** Each `@WebSocketController` class compiles to a module implementing the `Channel` behaviour (analogous to Phoenix's `Phoenix.Channel`). The `@OnConnect` method becomes `join/3`, `@OnDisconnect` becomes `terminate/2`, and `@OnMessage(event)` methods become `handle_in/3` clauses pattern-matched on the event name.
1843: 
1844: ---
1845: 
1846: ### Broadcasting
1847: 
1848: ```kotlin
1849: // From within a channel handler
1850: socket.broadcast("new_notification", notificationPayload)
1851: // Sends to all sockets currently subscribed to the same topic
1852: 
1853: // From outside a channel (e.g., from a service when a new notification arrives)
1854: @Service
1855: class NotificationService(private val channelBroadcaster: ChannelBroadcaster) {
1856: 
1857:     fun createAndNotify(userId: String, notification: Notification) {
1858:         val saved = notificationRepository.save(notification)
1859:         // Broadcast to all of this user's connected clients
1860:         channelBroadcaster.broadcast(
1861:             topic = "notification:$userId",
1862:             event = "new_notification",
1863:             payload = NotificationPayload.from(saved)
1864:         )
1865:     }
1866: }
1867: ```
1868: 
1869: Broadcasting to a topic sends the message to the `PubSub` process associated with that topic. All channel processes subscribed to the topic receive the message and forward it to their connected clients. This uses BEAM's `pg` (process groups) module under the hood — the same mechanism Phoenix PubSub uses.
1870: 
1871: ---
1872: 
1873: ### Phoenix.Presence Integration
1874: 
1875: ```kotlin
1876: @WebSocketController(topic = "room:{roomId}")
1877: class ChatChannel(private val presence: Presence) {
1878: 
1879:     @OnConnect
1880:     fun onJoin(socket: ChannelSocket, params: Map<String, String>): Ok<ChannelState> | Err<String> {
1881:         val user = socket.assigns["currentUser"] as? User
1882:             ?: return Err("Unauthorized")
1883: 
1884:         // Track this connection in presence
1885:         presence.track(socket, user.id, mapOf(
1886:             "name" to user.name,
1887:             "joinedAt" to BEAMTime.now()
1888:         ))
1889: 
1890:         // Push current presence state to joining client
1891:         socket.push("presence_state", presence.list(socket.topic))
1892: 
1893:         return Ok(ChannelState(roomId = socket.topicParams["roomId"]!!, userId = user.id))
1894:     }
1895: 
1896:     // Presence diffs are automatically pushed to all subscribers
1897:     // when any client joins or leaves. No explicit handler needed.
1898: }
1899: ```
1900: 
1901: Ping's `Presence` module wraps `Phoenix.Presence` directly. The BEAM-level implementation is unchanged — only the API surface is KorE-idiomatic. Presence tracks which users are connected to which topics, handles CRDT-based conflict resolution for distributed systems, and automatically broadcasts join/leave diffs to all subscribers.
1902: 
1903: ---
1904: 
1905: ### Complete Example: Real-Time Notification Channel
1906: 
1907: ```kotlin
1908: // notification_channel.kore
1909: data class ChannelState(
1910:     val userId: String,
1911:     val roomId: String? = null
1912: )
1913: 
1914: data class MarkReadPayload(val notificationId: String)
1915: data class NotificationPayload(
1916:     val id: String,
1917:     val type: String,
1918:     val title: String,
1919:     val body: String,
1920:     val createdAt: Long
1921: ) {
1922:     companion object {
1923:         fun from(n: Notification): NotificationPayload =
1924:             NotificationPayload(n.id, n.type, n.title, n.body, n.createdAt)
1925:     }
1926: }
1927: 
1928: @WebSocketController(topic = "notification:{userId}")
1929: class NotificationChannel(
1930:     private val notificationService: NotificationService,
1931:     private val presence: Presence
1932: ) {
1933: 
1934:     @OnConnect
1935:     fun onJoin(
1936:         socket: ChannelSocket,
1937:         params: Map<String, String>
1938:     ): Ok<ChannelState> | Err<String> {
1939:         val currentUser = socket.assigns["currentUser"] as? User
1940:             ?: return Err("Unauthorized: missing authentication")
1941: 
1942:         val topicUserId = socket.topicParams["userId"]
1943:             ?: return Err("Invalid topic")
1944: 
1945:         // Users can only subscribe to their own notification topic
1946:         if (currentUser.id != topicUserId) {
1947:             return Err("Unauthorized: cannot subscribe to another user's notifications")
1948:         }
1949: 
1950:         presence.track(socket, currentUser.id, mapOf(
1951:             "status" to "online",
1952:             "connectedAt" to BEAMTime.now()
1953:         ))
1954: 
1955:         val unread = notificationService.findUnread(currentUser.id)
1956:         socket.push("initial_notifications", mapOf("notifications" to unread.map(NotificationPayload::from)))
1957: 
1958:         return Ok(ChannelState(userId = currentUser.id))
1959:     }
1960: 
1961:     @OnDisconnect
1962:     fun onLeave(socket: ChannelSocket, reason: LeaveReason, state: ChannelState) {
1963:         Logger.info("Notification channel disconnected for user ${state.userId}: $reason")
1964:     }
1965: 
1966:     @OnMessage("mark_read")
1967:     fun onMarkRead(
1968:         socket: ChannelSocket,
1969:         payload: MarkReadPayload,
1970:         state: ChannelState
1971:     ): Ok<ChannelState> | Err<String> {
1972:         return when (notificationService.markRead(state.userId, payload.notificationId)) {
1973:             is Ok -> {
1974:                 socket.reply(.ok, mapOf("id" to payload.notificationId))
1975:                 Ok(state)
1976:             }
1977:             is Err -> Err("Notification not found or already read")
1978:         }
1979:     }
1980: 
1981:     @OnMessage("mark_all_read")
1982:     fun onMarkAllRead(
1983:         socket: ChannelSocket,
1984:         payload: Map<String, Any?>,
1985:         state: ChannelState
1986:     ): Ok<ChannelState> | Err<String> {
1987:         notificationService.markAllRead(state.userId)
1988:         socket.reply(.ok, mapOf("cleared" to true))
1989:         return Ok(state)
1990:     }
1991: }
1992: ```
1993: 
1994: The WebSocket transport upgrade happens in the endpoint pipeline before the channel router dispatches to `NotificationChannel`. The channel router matches topics using the same pattern-matching router as the HTTP router, generating efficient BEAM function clauses.
1995: 
1996: ---
1997: 
1998: ## 10.9 — Security
1999: 
2000: ### Authentication Pipeline
2001: 
2002: Security in Ping is not a magic container context — it is middleware that enriches `PingConn.assigns`. There is no `SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication()` global. There is `conn.assigns["currentUser"]`. The difference matters: per-request isolation is structural, not conventional.
2003: 
2004: The authentication flow:
2005: 
2006: 1. `AuthMiddleware` reads the `Authorization` header
2007: 2. It verifies the JWT and extracts claims
2008: 3. It calls `userService.findById(claims.subject)` to load the user
2009: 4. It sets `conn.assigns["currentUser"] = user`
2010: 5. Downstream controllers access `conn.currentUser`
2011: 
2012: If authentication fails, `AuthMiddleware` halts the pipeline and returns 401. Unauthenticated controllers never run.
2013: 
2014: ---
2015: 
2016: ### JWT Authentication Built-In
2017: 
2018: ```kotlin
2019: // config/application.kore.yml
2020: ping:
2021:   security:
2022:     jwt:
2023:       secret: ${JWT_SECRET}
2024:       expiry: 3600   # seconds
2025:       issuer: "my-app"
2026:       algorithm: HS256
2027: 
2028: // auth_middleware.kore
2029: class AuthMiddleware(
2030:     private val jwtService: JwtService,
2031:     private val userRepository: UserRepository
2032: ) : Middleware {
2033: 
2034:     override fun call(conn: PingConn): PingConn {
2035:         val token = extractToken(conn) ?: return conn  // unauthenticated, pass through
2036: 
2037:         return when (val claims = jwtService.verify(token)) {
2038:             is Err -> conn
2039:                 .putStatus(401)
2040:                 .json(ProblemDetail("about:blank", "Invalid Token", 401, claims.error.message))
2041:                 .halt()
2042:             is Ok -> when (val user = userRepository.findById(claims.value.subject)) {
2043:                 is Err -> conn
2044:                     .putStatus(401)
2045:                     .json(ProblemDetail("about:blank", "User Not Found", 401))
2046:                     .halt()
2047:                 is Ok -> conn.assign("currentUser", user.value)
2048:             }
2049:         }
2050:     }
2051: 
2052:     private fun extractToken(conn: PingConn): String? =
2053:         conn.headers.get("Authorization")
2054:             ?.takeIf { it.startsWith("Bearer ") }
2055:             ?.removePrefix("Bearer ")
2056: }
2057: 
2058: // jwt_service.kore
2059: @Service
2060: class JwtService(private val config: JwtConfig) {
2061: 
2062:     fun sign(userId: String, roles: List<String>): String =
2063:         JWT.create()
2064:             .withSubject(userId)
2065:             .withClaim("roles", roles)
2066:             .withIssuer(config.issuer)
2067:             .withExpiresAt(BEAMTime.now() + config.expiry.seconds)
2068:             .sign(Algorithm.HMAC256(config.secret))
2069: 
2070:     fun verify(token: String): Ok<JwtClaims> | Err<JwtError> =
2071:         runCatching {
2072:             val decoded = JWT.require(Algorithm.HMAC256(config.secret))
2073:                 .withIssuer(config.issuer)
2074:                 .build()
2075:                 .verify(token)
2076:             Ok(JwtClaims(
2077:                 subject = decoded.subject,
2078:                 roles = decoded.getClaim("roles").asList(String::class.java)
2079:             ))
2080:         }.getOrElse { e -> Err(JwtError(e.message ?: "Token verification failed")) }
2081: }
2082: ```
2083: 
2084: ---
2085: 
2086: ### Role-Based Authorization DSL
2087: 
2088: ```kotlin
2089: // Role-based route protection in the router
2090: router {
2091:     pipeline(.api) {
2092:         plug(JsonParser)
2093:         plug(AuthMiddleware)
2094:     }
2095: 
2096:     pipeline(.admin_api) {
2097:         pipe_through(.api)
2098:         plug(RequireRole(.admin))
2099:     }
2100: 
2101:     scope("/api/v1") {
2102:         pipe_through(.api)
2103:         resources("/users", UserController)
2104:         resources("/posts", PostController)
2105: 
2106:         scope("/admin") {
2107:             pipe_through(.admin_api)
2108:             resources("/users", AdminUserController)
2109:             resources("/settings", AdminSettingsController)
2110:         }
2111:     }
2112: }
2113: 
2114: // require_role.kore
2115: class RequireRole(private val requiredRole: Atom) : Middleware {
2116:     override fun call(conn: PingConn): PingConn {
2117:         val user = conn.currentUser
2118:             ?: return conn
2119:                 .putStatus(401)
2120:                 .json(ProblemDetail.unauthorized())
2121:                 .halt()
2122: 
2123:         if (!user.hasRole(requiredRole.name)) {
2124:             return conn
2125:                 .putStatus(403)
2126:                 .json(ProblemDetail("about:blank", "Forbidden", 403,
2127:                     "Role '${requiredRole.name}' required"))
2128:                 .halt()
2129:         }
2130: 
2131:         return conn
2132:     }
2133: }
2134: ```
2135: 
2136: For method-level authorization, Ping provides `@Secured` and `@PreAuthorize`:
2137: 
2138: ```kotlin
2139: @RestController
2140: class AdminUserController(private val userService: UserService) {
2141: 
2142:     @Get
2143:     @Secured("admin")
2144:     fun index(): List<UserResponse> { ... }
2145: 
2146:     @Delete("/{id}")
2147:     @PreAuthorize("hasRole('admin') or #id == currentUser.id")
2148:     fun delete(@PathVariable id: String) { ... }
2149: }
2150: ```
2151: 
2152: `@Secured` compiles to a middleware added to the specific handler's pipeline. `@PreAuthorize` with SpEL-like expressions compiles to a guard function that receives `conn.assigns` as context. The expression `#id == currentUser.id` compiles to a comparison between the path variable `id` and `conn.currentUser.id`.
2153: 
2154: ---
2155: 
2156: ### Per-Process SecurityContext
2157: 
2158: There is no `SecurityContextHolder`. There is `conn.currentUser`. This is not a downgrade — it is structurally superior.
2159: 
2160: In Spring, `SecurityContextHolder` uses thread-local storage. If you spawn a new thread (for async processing, scheduled tasks, etc.), you must manually transfer the security context to the new thread. This is a common source of bugs — `getAuthentication()` returns null in async code because the security context was not copied.
2161: 
2162: In Ping, the `currentUser` is in `conn.assigns`. The `conn` is passed explicitly through the pipeline. There is no ambient context to forget to copy. If you spawn a `Task` inside a controller and need the current user, you capture it from `conn` explicitly:
2163: 
2164: ```kotlin
2165: @Get("/{id}/export")
2166: fun export(@PathVariable id: String): Response {
2167:     val user = conn.currentUser ?: throw UnauthorizedException()
2168: 
2169:     // Explicitly pass user to the async task — no ambient context
2170:     val task = Task {
2171:         exportService.generateReport(id, requestedBy = user.id)
2172:     }
2173: 
2174:     return Response.accepted(mapOf("taskId" to task.id))
2175: }
2176: ```
2177: 
2178: The explicitness is a feature. Security-relevant context (who is making this request) is always visible in the code, never hidden in a thread-local.
2179: 
2180: ---
2181: 
2182: ## 10.10 — Observability and Actuator
2183: 
2184: ### Auto-Generated Endpoints
2185: 
2186: `@PingApplication` automatically registers an actuator-equivalent at `/ping/`:
2187: 
2188: ```
2189: GET /ping/health      — health check (aggregates all health indicators)
2190: GET /ping/metrics     — Prometheus-compatible metrics
2191: GET /ping/info        — application info (version, config subset)
2192: GET /ping/processes   — BEAM process count, memory
2193: GET /ping/supervisor  — supervision tree status
2194: ```
2195: 
2196: These endpoints are served by a separate lightweight endpoint on a different port (default: 4001) to prevent actuator traffic from affecting application traffic and to allow network-level firewall rules to restrict actuator access.
2197: 
2198: ---
2199: 
2200: ### BEAM Telemetry Integration
2201: 
2202: Spring Actuator pulls metrics from MBeans, Micrometer registries, and custom actuator endpoints. Ping uses `:telemetry` — the BEAM-native structured event system — as its metrics backbone. `:telemetry` is the standard for Phoenix, Ecto, and the broader BEAM ecosystem. Every significant operation emits a telemetry event.
2203: 
2204: ```kotlin
2205: // Ping automatically emits these telemetry events:
2206: // [:ping, :request, :start]  — when request processing begins
2207: // [:ping, :request, :stop]   — when request processing ends
2208: // [:ping, :request, :exception] — when request process crashes
2209: 
2210: // Attaching a custom telemetry handler
2211: @Component
2212: class RequestMetricsCollector {
2213: 
2214:     @PostConstruct
2215:     fun attach() {
2216:         Telemetry.attach(
2217:             "request-metrics",
2218:             listOf(listOf(.ping, .request, .stop))
2219:         ) { eventName, measurements, metadata, _ ->
2220:             Metrics.histogram(
2221:                 "ping.request.duration",
2222:                 measurements["duration"] as Long,
2223:                 Tags.of(
2224:                     "method" to (metadata["conn"] as PingConn).method.name,
2225:                     "status" to (metadata["conn"] as PingConn).status.toString(),
2226:                     "route" to (metadata["route"] as String)
2227:                 )
2228:             )
2229:         }
2230:     }
2231: }
2232: ```
2233: 
2234: Built-in metrics (auto-collected):
2235: - `ping.request.duration` — histogram, tagged by method/status/route
2236: - `ping.request.count` — counter, tagged by method/status
2237: - `beam.process.count` — gauge, from `:erlang.system_info(:process_count)`
2238: - `beam.memory.total` — gauge, from `:erlang.memory(:total)`
2239: - `beam.memory.processes` — gauge
2240: - `beam.run_queue` — gauge, scheduler run queue length
2241: - `beam.gc.count` — counter, GC events
2242: - `db.query.duration` — histogram, tagged by repo/query
2243:

2247:

2250: @Component
2251: class DatabaseHealthIndicator(
2252:     private val userRepository: UserRepository
2253: ) : HealthIndicator {
2254: 
2255:     override fun health(): Health {
2256:         return when (userRepository.ping()) {
2257:             is Ok -> Health.up()
2258:                 .withDetail("database", "PostgreSQL")
2259:                 .withDetail("responseTime", "${measureMs { userRepository.ping() }}ms")
2260:                 .build()
2261:             is Err -> Health.down()
2262:                 .withDetail("error", "Database unreachable")
2263:                 .build()
2264:         }
2265:     }

2267:

2319: ---
2320: 
2321: ### BEAM Observer and `:recon` Integration
2322: 
2323: Ping integrates with the BEAM's built-in observability tools:
2324: 
2325: ```kotlin
2326: // Enable Observer web UI (Phoenix LiveDashboard equivalent)
2327: @PingApplication(
2328:     observability = Observability(
2329:         observer = true,         // Enable :observer web interface
2330:         recon = true,            // Enable :recon_web interface
2331:         dashboard = true         // Enable Ping Live Dashboard at /ping/dashboard
2332:     )
2333: )
2334: class MyApp
2335: ```
2336: 
2337: The Ping Live Dashboard provides real-time visualization of:
2338: - Request throughput and latency percentiles
2339: - BEAM process count and memory usage
2340: - Supervisor tree health
2341: - Recent errors with stack traces
2342: - Database query performance
2343: 
2344: This is equivalent to Spring Boot Admin + Spring Actuator + a profiler, built on BEAM's native tooling (`:observer`, `:recon`, `:telemetry`).
2345: 
2346: ---
2347: 
2348: ## 10.11 — The Ping Application: Startup and Supervision
2349: 
2350: ### `@PingApplication`
2351: 
2352: ```kotlin
2353: // main.kore
2354: @PingApplication(
2355:     port = 4000,
2356:     environment = Environment.DEV,
2357:     config = "config/application.kore.yml"
2358: )
2359: fun main() {
2360:     Ping.start()
2361: }
2362: ```
2363: 
2364: `@PingApplication` is the single entry point annotation. It triggers the generation of the full OTP application, supervision tree, and all required infrastructure. The `main()` function body is minimal — `Ping.start()` hands off to the generated OTP application.
2365: 
2366: ---
2367: 
2368: ### Generated OTP Application
2369: 
2370: The compiler generates an OTP application module:
2371: 
2372: ```kotlin
2373: // Generated: 'KorE.MyApp.Application'
2374: @BEAMModule("KorE.MyApp.Application")
2375: class MyAppApplication : OTPApplication() {
2376: 
2377:     override fun start(type: StartType, args: List<Dynamic>): Ok<Pid> | Err<Dynamic> {
2378:         val children = listOf(
2379:             childSpec(MyApp.Supervisor, strategy = .oneForOne)
2380:         )
2381:         return Supervisor.startLink(children, strategy = .oneForOne)
2382:     }
2383: }
2384: ```
2385: 
2386: The root supervisor is `MyApp.Supervisor`, also generated. Its children are assembled from:
2387: 1. The Ping endpoint infrastructure (acceptors, connection pool)
2388: 2. All `@Service` and `@Repository` components found during compilation
2389: 3. The database connection pool (if a database is configured)
2390: 4. The channel socket server (if `@WebSocketController`s are present)
2391: 5. The PubSub server (if broadcasting is used)
2392: 
2393: ---
2394: 
2395: ### The Full Generated Supervision Tree
2396: 
2397: ```
2398: MyApp.Supervisor (strategy: :oneForOne)
2399: │
2400: ├── Ping.Endpoint.Supervisor (strategy: :oneForAll)
2401: │   │   (oneForAll: if acceptor dies, restart connection pool too)
2402: │   ├── Ping.Cowboy.Acceptor (HTTP/1.1 + HTTP/2 acceptor, port 4000)
2403: │   ├── Ping.ConnectionPool (DynamicSupervisor for request processes)
2404: │   └── Ping.ChannelServer (WebSocket channel router, if applicable)
2405: │
2406: ├── MyApp.Services.Supervisor (strategy: :oneForOne)
2407: │   │   (oneForOne: service failures are isolated)
2408: │   ├── UserRepository (GenServer, name: :KorE_UserRepository)
2409: │   ├── SessionService (GenServer, name: :KorE_SessionService)
2410: │   ├── CacheService (GenServer, name: :KorE_CacheService)
2411: │   └── AuditService (GenServer, name: :KorE_AuditService)
2412: │
2413: ├── MyApp.Database.Supervisor (strategy: :restForOne)
2414: │   │   (restForOne: pool monitor must restart after pool restarts)
2415: │   ├── Database.ConnectionPool (postgrex pool)
2416: │   └── Database.QueryMonitor (telemetry monitor)
2417: │
2418: ├── Ping.PubSub (Phoenix.PubSub, for channel broadcasting)
2419: ├── Ping.Presence (Phoenix.Presence, if presence is used)
2420: │
2421: └── Ping.Actuator.Endpoint (HTTP endpoint on port 4001 for /ping/*)
2422: ```
2423: 
2424: The supervisor tree is deterministic and compiler-generated. The developer can inspect it in `generated/supervision_tree.kore`, which is always up to date with the current set of annotations in the codebase.
2425: 
2426: To override the generated tree (e.g., to add a custom supervisor, change restart strategies), create `supervision_tree.kore` at the project root:
2427: 
2428: ```kotlin
2429: // supervision_tree.kore — override generated tree
2430: @PingSupervisionTree
2431: fun supervisionTree(): SupervisorSpec = supervisor {
2432:     strategy(.oneForOne)
2433: 
2434:     // Use the generated endpoint supervisor as-is
2435:     child(Ping.Endpoint.Supervisor)
2436: 
2437:     // Custom supervisor for our services
2438:     child(supervisor("services") {
2439:         strategy(.oneForOne)
2440:         child(UserRepository)
2441:         child(UserService)
2442:         child(EmailService)
2443:     })
2444: 
2445:     // Add a custom worker
2446:     child(MyApp.BackgroundJobWorker, restart = .permanent)
2447: 
2448:     // Database with custom pool size
2449:     child(Database.ConnectionPool, poolSize = 20)
2450: }
2451: ```
2452: 
2453: ---
2454: 
2455: ### Configuration
2456: 
2457: **`config/application.kore.yml`** is the Spring-familiar configuration format:
2458: 
2459: ```yaml
2460: # config/application.kore.yml
2461: ping:
2462:   port: 4000
2463:   secret_key_base: ${SECRET_KEY_BASE}
2464: 
2465:   security:
2466:     jwt:
2467:       secret: ${JWT_SECRET}
2468:       expiry: 3600
2469:       issuer: "my-app"
2470: 
2471: database:
2472:   url: ${DATABASE_URL}
2473:   pool_size: 10
2474: 
2475: logging:
2476:   level: info
2477:   format: json  # or "text" for development
2478: 
2479: ---
2480: # config/application-dev.kore.yml (dev profile overrides)
2481: ping:
2482:   port: 4000
2483: 
2484: database:
2485:   url: "postgres://localhost/myapp_dev"
2486:   pool_size: 5
2487: 
2488: logging:
2489:   level: debug
2490:   format: text
2491: ```
2492: 
2493: Profile activation:
2494: 
2495: ```bash
2496: PING_ENV=dev ./myapp
2497: PING_ENV=prod ./myapp
2498: ```
2499: 
2500: Or at compile time:
2501: 
2502: ```kotlin
2503: @PingApplication(environment = Environment.PROD)
2504: fun main() { Ping.start() }
2505: ```
2506: 
2507: The environment profile system compiles to `Mix.env()` / `Application.get_env/2` under the hood. `application.kore.yml` compiles to `config/config.exs` and environment-specific overrides compile to `config/{env}.exs`. The YAML format is the developer-facing surface; the Erlang config system is what runs.
2508: 
2509: ---
2510: 
2511: ### Hot Code Reload
2512: 
2513: BEAM supports hot code reload — updating running code without restarting the system. This is more sophisticated than Spring Boot DevTools' class reloading.
2514: 
2515: In development mode, Ping monitors source files and recompiles changed modules. Changed modules are loaded into the running system via BEAM's code server. Running processes that are in the middle of a call to the old module complete with the old code; new calls use the new code. This is safe — BEAM's code server keeps two versions of a module in memory simultaneously during upgrades.
2516: 
2517: ```kotlin
2518: // config/application-dev.kore.yml
2519: ping:
2520:   hot_reload:
2521:     enabled: true
2522:     watch_paths:
2523:       - "src/"
2524:       - "lib/"
2525:     ignore_paths:
2526:       - "src/test/"
2527: ```
2528: 
2529: For production hot upgrades, Ping supports OTP release upgrades via `appup` files — the same mechanism used by Erlang/OTP systems that have been running continuously for years. This is beyond the scope of most web frameworks. It is a BEAM feature, and Ping exposes it.
2530: 
2531: ---
2532: 
2533: ### Complete Application Entry Point
2534: 
2535: ```kotlin
2536: // main.kore — complete application entry point
2537: 
2538: @PingApplication(
2539:     port = 4000,
2540:     config = "config/application.kore.yml"
2541: )
2542: fun main() {
2543:     Logger.info("Starting MyApp on port 4000")
2544:     Logger.info("Environment: ${Ping.environment()}")
2545:     Logger.info("BEAM version: ${BEAMInfo.oTPVersion()}")
2546:     Ping.start()
2547: }
2548: 
2549: // The compiler generates this from the above + all annotations found:
2550: //
2551: // MyApp.Supervisor (oneForOne)
2552: // ├── Ping.Endpoint (port 4000)
2553: // │   ├── HTTP Acceptor
2554: // │   ├── ConnectionPool (DynamicSupervisor)
2555: // │   └── ChannelServer
2556: // ├── MyApp.Services (oneForOne)
2557: // │   ├── UserRepository
2558: // │   ├── SessionService
2559: // │   ├── CacheService
2560: // │   └── AuditService
2561: // ├── Database.Supervisor (restForOne)

2563: // │   └── Database.QueryMonitor
2564: // ├── Ping.PubSub
2565: // └── Ping.Actuator (port 4001)
2566: 
2567: // config/application.kore.yml (development)
2568: // ping:
2569: //   port: 4000
2570: //   hot_reload:
2571: //     enabled: true

2585: 
2586: ---
2587: 
2588: ## 10.12 — Language Feature Requirements Inventory
2589: 
2590: This section is a precise inventory of what Ping requires from the KorE compiler and language. Each item states what it is, what it must generate, and which compiler phase handles it.
2591: 
2592: ---
2593: 
2594: ### 1. Annotation Processing Model
2595: 
2596: **What it is:** Annotations like `@RestController`, `@GetMapping`, `@Service`, `@Autowired` must be processed at compile time to generate BEAM modules, routing tables, and supervision tree entries.
2597: 
2598: **What it must generate:**
2599: - `@RestController` → BEAM module with one exported function per `@Get`/`@Post`/etc. annotated method
2600: - `@Service` → GenServer module with `init/1`, `handle_call/3`, `handle_cast/2`, `terminate/2`; registration in service supervisor child spec
2601: - `@Repository` → GenServer wrapping a connection pool; child spec in database supervisor
2602: - `@Component` → Plain BEAM module; registration in DI resolver table for injection
2603: - `@WebSocketController` → Channel behaviour module with `join/3`, `handle_in/3`, `terminate/2`
2604: - `@PingApplication` → OTP application module, full supervision tree, mix.exs/rebar.config
2605: 
2606: **Compiler phase:** Annotation processing runs as a dedicated pass between parsing and type checking. Annotations that transform class structure (e.g., `@Service` which rewrites instance fields to GenServer state) must run before type checking so that the type checker sees the transformed structure.
2607: 
2608: **Implementation note:** Annotation processors in KorE are macro-like compiler plugins registered in `kore.toml`. The compiler provides a `CompilerContext` API that annotation processors use to read annotated elements, query types, and emit new module definitions. Annotation processors cannot modify existing source — they emit new generated files to `generated/`.
2609: 
2610: ---
2611: 
2612: ### 2. Route Compilation
2613: 
2614: **What it is:** The router DSL (`router { scope("/api") { get("/users/{id}", ...) } }`) must be evaluated at compile time to produce a routing module.
2615: 
2616: **What it must generate:**
2617: 
2618: A BEAM module `'KorE.MyApp.Router'` with pattern-matched function clauses:
2619: 
2620: ```erlang
2621: % Generated Erlang
2622: route(Conn = #{method := <<"GET">>, path_segments := [<<"api">>, <<"v1">>, <<"users">>, Id]}) ->
2623:     Conn2 = maps:put(path_params, #{<<"id">> => Id}, Conn),
2624:     pipeline([log, json_parser, auth], Conn2,
2625:              fun(C) -> 'KorE.UserController':show(C) end);
2626: route(Conn = #{method := <<"POST">>, path_segments := [<<"api">>, <<"v1">>, <<"users">>]}) ->
2627:     pipeline([log, json_parser, auth], Conn,
2628:              fun(C) -> 'KorE.UserController':create(C) end);
2629: ```
2630: 
2631: The routing trie is compiled to a decision tree of pattern matches. The compiler uses a trie-building algorithm (similar to Phoenix's Router) to minimize the number of comparisons on the hot path.
2632: 
2633: **Compiler phase:** Route compilation is a compile-time evaluation pass. The router DSL is evaluated as a KorE program at compile time, producing a `RouteTable` data structure. The `RouteTable` is then code-generated into the `'KorE.Router'` Erlang module.
2634: 
2635: **Conflict detection:** The compiler validates the route table for conflicts (two routes matching the same method + path) and emits `KE2001: Duplicate route` as a compile error.
2636: 
2637: ---
2638: 
2639: ### 3. Parameter Binding
2640: 
2641: **What it is:** `@PathVariable`, `@RequestParam`, `@RequestBody`, `@RequestHeader` annotations on controller method parameters must be compiled to extraction code that reads from `PingConn`.
2642: 
2643: **What it must generate:**
2644: 
2645: For a method `fun show(@PathVariable id: String, @RequestParam page: Int?)`:
2646: 
2647: ```kotlin
2648: // Generated binding code (conceptual KorE)
2649: fun show_binding(conn: PingConn): PingConn {
2650:     val id: String = conn.pathParams["id"]
2651:         ?: return conn.putStatus(400)
2652:             .json(ProblemDetail.badRequest("Missing path variable: id"))
2653:             .halt()
2654: 
2655:     val page: Int? = conn.queryParams["page"]
2656:         ?.firstOrNull()
2657:         ?.toIntOrNull()
2658: 
2659:     return UserController.show(conn, id, page)
2660: }
2661: ```
2662: 
2663: For `@RequestBody request: CreateUserRequest`:
2664: 
2665: ```kotlin
2666: val request: CreateUserRequest = when (val body = conn.body) {
2667:     is Body.Parsed<*> -> body.value as? CreateUserRequest
2668:         ?: return conn.putStatus(400).json(ProblemDetail.badRequest("Body type mismatch")).halt()
2669:     else -> return conn.putStatus(400).json(ProblemDetail.badRequest("Body not parsed")).halt()
2670: }
2671: ```
2672: 
2673: **Compiler phase:** Parameter binding code generation is part of the controller compilation pass. Each annotated controller method is wrapped in a generated binding function. The binding function is what the router calls; the binding function calls the controller method after extracting and coercing parameters.
2674: 
2675: **Type coercion table:**
2676: 
2677: | Target type | Coercion | Failure behavior |
2678: |-------------|----------|-----------------|
2679: | `String` | Identity | Never fails |
2680: | `Int` | `toIntOrNull()` | 400 if null |
2681: | `Long` | `toLongOrNull()` | 400 if null |
2682: | `Double` | `toDoubleOrNull()` | 400 if null |
2683: | `Boolean` | `toBooleanStrictOrNull()` | 400 if null |
2684: | `UUID` | `UUID.fromString()` | 400 if throws |
2685: | `T?` | Nullable — coerce if present, null if absent | Never fails |
2686: 
2687: ---
2688: 
2689: ### 4. Middleware Pipeline Composition
2690: 
2691: **What it is:** Pipeline declarations (`pipeline(.api) { plug(A); plug(B) }`) must be compiled to efficient pipeline execution code.
2692: 
2693: **What it must generate:**
2694: 
2695: Two strategies are available:
2696: 
2697: **Strategy A: Runtime list** — Store middleware as a list, fold at request time.
2698: 
2699: ```kotlin
2700: val apiPipeline: List<Middleware> = listOf(
2701:     RequestLogger.instance,
2702:     JsonParser.instance,
2703:     AuthMiddleware.instance
2704: )
2705: 
2706: fun runPipeline(conn: PingConn): PingConn =
2707:     apiPipeline.fold(conn) { c, mw -> if (c.halted) c else mw.call(c) }
2708: ```
2709: 
2710: **Strategy B: Compile-time inlining** — Small, known pipelines can be inlined:
2711: 
2712: ```kotlin
2713: // Compiler generates this from pipeline(.api) { plug(A); plug(B); plug(C) }
2714: fun runApiPipeline(conn: PingConn): PingConn {
2715:     val c1 = if (conn.halted) conn else A.call(conn)
2716:     val c2 = if (c1.halted) c1 else B.call(c1)
2717:     val c3 = if (c2.halted) c2 else C.call(c2)
2718:     return c3
2719: }
2720: ```
2721: 
2722: Strategy B avoids the list allocation and fold overhead on the hot path. The compiler should choose Strategy B for pipelines with ≤8 middlewares (configurable), falling back to Strategy A for longer pipelines.
2723: 
2724: **Compiler phase:** Pipeline composition is resolved at route compilation time, when the full set of middlewares for each route is known. Pipelines are inlined into the generated routing function.
2725: 
2726: ---
2727: 
2728: ### 5. DI Resolution
2729: 
2730: **What it is:** Constructor parameters and `@Autowired` fields annotated on `@RestController`, `@Service`, `@Component`, and `@Repository` classes must be resolved at application startup.
2731: 
2732: **What it must generate:**
2733: 
2734: A `ServiceRegistry` module that maps type names to instances:
2735: 
2736: ```kotlin
2737: // Generated: 'KorE.MyApp.ServiceRegistry'
2738: object ServiceRegistry {
2739:     val userRepository: UserRepository by lazy {
2740:         GenServer.call(:'KorE.UserRepository', .get_instance) as UserRepository
2741:     }
2742:     val userService: UserService by lazy {
2743:         // UserService depends on UserRepository and EventBus
2744:         GenServer.call(:'KorE.UserService', .get_instance) as UserService
2745:     }
2746:     val userController: UserController by lazy {
2747:         UserController(userService)  // stateless, no GenServer
2748:     }
2749: }
2750: ```
2751: 
2752: The DI graph is computed at compile time. Circular dependencies are detected during annotation processing and reported as `KE4001: Circular dependency: UserService → UserRepository → UserService`.
2753: 
2754: **Compiler phase:** DI graph resolution is an annotation processing pass. The compiler builds a directed graph of dependencies from constructor parameters and `@Autowired` annotations. Topological sort determines initialization order. The `ServiceRegistry` is generated with dependencies initialized in the correct order.
2755: 
2756: ---
2757: 
2758: ### 6. Serialization
2759: 
2760: **What it is:** Controller return values (data classes, lists, primitive types) must be serialized to JSON (or other negotiated format) without explicit serializer calls.
2761: 
2762: **What it must generate:**
2763: 
2764: For each `data class` used as a controller return type, the compiler generates a serializer module:
2765: 
2766: ```kotlin
2767: // Generated for UserResponse data class
2768: object UserResponseSerializer {
2769:     fun toJson(value: UserResponse): ByteArray =
2770:         buildJsonObject {
2771:             put("id", value.id)
2772:             put("email", value.email)
2773:             put("name", value.name)
2774:             put("createdAt", value.createdAt)
2775:         }.toByteArray()
2776: 
2777:     fun fromJson(bytes: ByteArray): Ok<UserResponse> | Err<DeserializationError> =
2778:         runCatching {
2779:             val obj = parseJsonObject(bytes)
2780:             Ok(UserResponse(
2781:                 id = obj.getString("id"),
2782:                 email = obj.getString("email"),
2783:                 name = obj.getString("name"),
2784:                 createdAt = obj.getLong("createdAt")
2785:             ))
2786:         }.getOrElse { e -> Err(DeserializationError(e.message)) }
2787: }
2788: ```
2789: 
2790: Serializers are generated at compile time. No reflection. No runtime introspection. The serializer module is called by the controller wrapper generated in the parameter binding phase.
2791: 
2792: **Null handling:** Null fields in data classes serialize as JSON `null`. Use `T?` types to allow null fields; non-nullable fields that are null at serialization time throw a compile-detected warning (the type system should prevent this, but defensive runtime checks are generated for `Dynamic` interop paths).
2793: 
2794: **Custom serialization:** Annotate the class with `@JsonProperty`, `@JsonIgnore`, `@JsonSerialize(using = ...)` for customization.
2795: 
2796: **Compiler phase:** Serializer generation is an annotation processing pass that runs after type resolution, so all types of all fields are known. Serializers are emitted to `generated/serializers/`.
2797: 
2798: ---
2799: 
2800: ### 7. Validation Annotation Processing
2801: 
2802: **What it is:** `@NotBlank`, `@Size`, `@Email`, `@Min`, `@Max`, `@Pattern` annotations on `data class` fields must generate validation functions.
2803: 
2804: **What it must generate:**
2805: 
2806: For each `data class` with `@field:*` validation annotations, the compiler generates:
2807: 
2808: ```kotlin
2809: // Generated for CreateUserRequest
2810: object CreateUserRequestValidator {
2811:     fun validate(value: CreateUserRequest): List<Violation> = buildList {
2812:         if (value.email.isBlank())
2813:             add(Violation("email", "must not be blank"))
2814:         if (!value.email.matches(EMAIL_REGEX))
2815:             add(Violation("email", "must be a well-formed email address"))
2816:         if (value.password.isBlank())
2817:             add(Violation("password", "must not be blank"))
2818:         if (value.password.length < 8 || value.password.length > 100)
2819:             add(Violation("password", "size must be between 8 and 100"))
2820:         // ... etc.
2821:     }
2822: }
2823: ```
2824: 
2825: The generated validator is a pure function — no reflection, no annotation inspection at runtime. Validation is compile-time code generation.
2826: 
2827: **Custom validators:** Custom `@Constraint` annotations require a `ConstraintValidator` implementation. The compiler generates a call to the validator's `isValid()` method in the generated validation function. If the `ConstraintValidator` has injected dependencies, its constructor is resolved via the DI system.
2828: 
2829: **Compiler phase:** Validation code generation is an annotation processing pass running after type resolution.
2830: 
2831: ---
2832: 
2833: ### 8. WebSocket Channel Code Generation
2834: 
2835: **What it is:** `@WebSocketController` annotated classes with `@OnConnect`, `@OnDisconnect`, `@OnMessage` annotated methods must be compiled to Phoenix Channel behaviour modules.
2836: 
2837: **What it must generate:**
2838: 
2839: ```erlang
2840: % Generated from @WebSocketController(topic = "notification:{userId}")
2841: -module('KorE.NotificationChannel').
2842: -behaviour('Elixir.Phoenix.Channel').
2843: -export([join/3, handle_in/3, handle_out/3, terminate/2]).
2844: 
2845: join(<<"notification:", UserId/binary>>, Params, Socket) ->
2846:     %% Calls KorE-generated onJoin wrapper
2847:     'KorE.NotificationChannel.Impl':on_join(Socket, Params, UserId);
2848: join(_, _, _Socket) ->
2849:     {error, #{reason => <<"invalid_topic">>}}.
2850: 
2851: handle_in(<<"mark_read">>, Payload, Socket) ->
2852:     'KorE.NotificationChannel.Impl':on_mark_read(Socket, Payload);
2853: handle_in(<<"mark_all_read">>, Payload, Socket) ->
2854:     'KorE.NotificationChannel.Impl':on_mark_all_read(Socket, Payload);
2855: handle_in(Event, _Payload, Socket) ->
2856:     {reply, {error, #{reason => <<"unknown_event">>, event => Event}}, Socket}.
2857: 
2858: terminate(Reason, Socket) ->
2859:     'KorE.NotificationChannel.Impl':on_leave(Socket, Reason).
2860: ```
2861: 
2862: The `Impl` module contains the KorE-compiled versions of the annotated methods.
2863: 
2864: **Compiler phase:** Channel code generation is an annotation processing pass.
2865: 
2866: ---
2867: 
2868: ### 9. PingConn and Its BEAM Representation
2869: 
2870: **What it is:** `PingConn` must be an efficient, immutable carrier type that is passed through all middleware and controller code.
2871: 
2872: **BEAM representation:** `PingConn` compiles to an Erlang map with atom keys. The decision to use a map (rather than a record) is deliberate:
2873: 
2874: - Maps are structurally shareable — `conn.copy(status = 200)` is a map update that shares unmodified keys
2875: - Maps support the open `assigns` field without type-level generics
2876: - Map pattern matching in BEAM is efficient for small maps (< ~32 keys) using hash array mapped tries
2877: 
2878: The fixed keys of `PingConn` are known at compile time:
2879: 
2880: ```erlang
2881: % PingConn BEAM representation
2882: #{
2883:     method     => <<"GET">>,
2884:     path       => <<"/api/v1/users/123">>,
2885:     path_params => #{<<"id">> => <<"123">>},
2886:     query_params => #{},
2887:     headers    => #{<<"content-type">> => <<"application/json">>},
2888:     body       => unread,
2889:     status     => 200,
2890:     resp_headers => #{},
2891:     resp_body  => <<>>,
2892:     halted     => false,
2893:     assigns    => #{},
2894:     private    => #{},
2895:     adapter    => {cowboy_adapter, ...}
2896: }
2897: ```
2898: 
2899: `PingConn.copy()` compiles to a map update expression, which in BEAM generates a `maps:update/3` call or, for known keys, a more efficient map literal with updated fields.
2900: 
2901: **Compiler phase:** `PingConn` is a compiler-known type. The compiler generates optimized map access and update code for `PingConn` field access and `copy()` calls.
2902: 
2903: ---
2904: 
2905: ### 10. What the Ping Runtime Library Provides vs. What the Compiler Generates
2906: 
2907: This boundary is important for understanding what is a language feature and what is a library:
2908: 
2909: **Compiler generates (compile-time):**
2910: - Router module with pattern-matched route clauses
2911: - Controller binding functions (parameter extraction, coercion, validation dispatch)
2912: - Serializer modules for all data classes used as controller return types
2913: - Validator modules for all data classes with validation annotations
2914: - GenServer modules for `@Service`/`@Repository` annotated classes
2915: - Channel behaviour modules for `@WebSocketController` annotated classes
2916: - Supervision tree specification module
2917: - OTP application module
2918: - `ServiceRegistry` module with resolved DI graph
2919: - `Routes` object with URL generation functions
2920: - `generated/supervision_tree.kore` documentation file
2921: 
2922: **Ping runtime library provides (pre-compiled BEAM modules shipped with Ping):**
2923: - `Ping.Endpoint` — cowboy-based HTTP/2 + WebSocket endpoint
2924: - `Ping.Router.run/2` — pipeline execution (Strategy A fallback)
2925: - `Ping.PingConn` — the `PingConn` module with helper functions (`halt/1`, `putStatus/2`, `json/2`, `assign/3`, etc.)
2926: - `Ping.JwtService` — JWT signing and verification (wraps `:joken` or `:jose`)
2927: - `Ping.ContentNegotiation` — content negotiation middleware
2928: - `Ping.JsonParser` — body parsing middleware (wraps `:jason`)
2929: - `Ping.Presence` — Phoenix.Presence wrapper with KorE API
2930: - `Ping.ChannelBroadcaster` — topic broadcast interface
2931: - `Ping.Actuator` — health endpoint infrastructure
2932: - `Ping.Telemetry` — telemetry attachment and metrics collection
2933: - `Ping.TestClient` — HTTP test client for integration tests
2934: 
2935: The boundary is: if it requires knowledge of your application's specific classes, routes, or types, the compiler generates it. If it is generic infrastructure that works for any Ping application, it is in the runtime library.
2936: 
2937: This boundary has a compiler tooling implication: the Ping runtime library is an ordinary KorE/Erlang dependency in `kore.toml`. It does not require any special compiler support. The compiler-generated code depends on the runtime library — not the other way around.
2938:
